Post-Quantum Zcash

Post-Quantum Zcash

This repository holds design work towards post-quantum security for Zcash: the candidate proof systems and commitment schemes, and the analyses that compare them. It will eventually include formal verification of the claims made about them. The book is the primary document. The models, data and notes that it draws on live beside it in this repository: the study of commitment schemes for Ragu is under ragu-pcs/, and the book’s Proof Systems section presents it.

Building the Lean package

The Lean package PQZcash is where the formal verification will live; it is empty so far. Building a Lean development re-elaborates every proof, so a successful build is the verification. Install elan, the Lean toolchain manager, which reads lean-toolchain and installs the pinned toolchain automatically. Then, from the repository root:

lake build --wfail   # verify every proof; --wfail makes warnings fail, as CI does

Proof Systems

The zero-knowledge proofs deployed in Zcash’s shielded protocols are not post-quantum. Sapling’s Groth16 proofs rest on pairings, and the Orchard protocol’s Halo 2 proofs rest on the discrete logarithm problem in the Pasta curves. A quantum adversary could forge either, and so could break the soundness of the shielded pools.

Ragu is a proof-carrying-data scheme built for Tachyon: each step proves a small circuit, and the steps’ proofs are folded into an accumulator rather than verified in full. Its polynomial commitment scheme is Pedersen commitments opened by an inner-product argument, the same family as Halo 2’s, and that is where its pre-quantum assumption lives. It is also what sets the size of its proofs and the cost of its prover and of its recursion. The chapters in this section ask what replacing that commitment scheme with a post-quantum one would cost, for the lattice-based and hash-based schemes that could do it.

Commitment Schemes for Ragu

This study prices Ragu as a proof-carrying-data scheme under each candidate commitment scheme, on the measures of The PCS Frontier: the compressed proof’s bytes, and two more chosen from eight, among them the prover’s work for one step’s commitments, for a fuse’s accumulation, and for a whole transaction, the merge circuit’s gates or the atoms it absorbs, the decider’s work, and the accumulator’s and a fuse’s peak memory. The candidates are:

  • Ragu’s Pedersen inner-product argument as deployed today, the pre-quantum baseline;
  • Akita (ePrint 2026/1983), a lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme over Module-SIS, priced under five choices of field and commitment modulus, from its own 128-bit field to the Pasta base field;
  • the hash-based schemes: WHIR over Pasta, over Goldilocks, and with Pasta claims in 64-bit limbs; a Plonky3-style FRI over Goldilocks; the Flock/Binius-style binary-field family, whose proof sizes come from FRI-Binius; and BitZ, which is Pasta-native through a binary field. Each is priced both under ARC accumulation and under its own recursion;
  • and Kishu, BitZ’s bit-level arithmetization with Akita as the backend, a draft.

The hash-based rows’ rate and grinding, the security floor, zero knowledge, and the hashes allowed in circuits are selectable. For each class, pre-quantum and post-quantum, the comparison marks the frontier: the configurations that nothing else in the class dominates on proof bytes, the two chosen measures, and three requirements. Native support for the Pasta base field is one requirement, since the Ironwood recovery circuit needs it; the others are the scheme’s assumption and whether a row needs only parameter changes.

No scheme has been selected. The comparison is an input to that choice, beside implementation experience with each route.

The PCS frontier is the interactive comparison. The study’s own material is in the repository’s ragu-pcs/ directory. There, pareto-model.py generates the comparison from the measurements under estimates/ and the models beside it, and WORKING-NOTES.md is the running log of what was done and what is open. Regenerating the Study’s Numbers says where each number comes from and how to redo it. The study’s longer write-ups are in the Kishu and Other Schemes sections: for Kishu, the zero-knowledge fold of a lattice accumulation step and the soundness statements; for the others, an Akita opening priced at a Pasta modulus and the soundness statement of the variant with Pasta claims.

The PCS Frontier

This page costs Ragu over a wide range of parameters — with its pre-quantum Pedersen-IPA decider, and adapted to various post-quantum PCD schemes. The lattice-based scheme Akita is considered under five field and modulus choices, and with an experimental BitZ-style arithmetization over it, called Kishu. For hash-based schemes, we consider: WHIR over Pasta, over Goldilocks, and with Pasta claims in 64‑bit limbs; a Plonky3-style FRI over Goldilocks; the Flock/Binius-style binary-field family; and BitZ, each with ARC accumulation and with its own recursion. A further experimental draft is Flock-style Boolean circuits over Akita's binary groups. This is commit 22eb745 of the model.

The frontier plot

Each point is one configuration. Its coordinates are compressed proof bytes and two measures chosen from the same eight: the accumulation prover; the prover work for one step's commitments; merge gates; the atoms that the merge circuit absorbs; the decider's verification work; the prover work for a whole transaction; the accumulator's memory; or the peak memory of a fuse. The hash-based rows' rate and grinding, the security floor, zero knowledge, and the hashes allowed in circuits (conventional only, or Poseidon 1.1 too) are selectable. The WHIR-type and Plonky3 families start unticked in the families list, since Akita beats them on every measure and their many rows crowd the picture.

Each class, pre-quantum (Pedersen-IPA) and post‑quantum (the rest), has its own frontier: the configurations of the class, among the selection above, that nothing else in the class dominates. A configuration dominates another when it is at least as good on six axes and better on at least one. The axes are compressed proof bytes, the selected second and third measures, and three requirements, described in the next section and under Parameter changes against design changes: native or relation Pasta arithmetic, the security assumption, and the changes a configuration needs. The table lists both frontiers, and each family's own frontier besides, marked "family" in the last column, so that every scheme's best configurations appear even where its class dominates it. Header size only adds bytes, the same to every row, so the control sets one header for all.

Pasta and the scheme assumption

Three things enter the dominance test as requirements rather than costs: the Pasta arithmetic that the Ironwood recovery circuit needs, the security assumption, and the changes to Ragu that a configuration needs, which a later section takes up. The table's Pasta arithmetic column says how each scheme realises the first:

  • native: a gate over Pasta's field (Pedersen-IPA, the Pasta variants of Akita, WHIR over Pasta and the limb hybrid, whose witness and merge circuit are over Pasta);
  • relation, limbs: the multiplication as an integer relation over committed digits, with the result and the quotient committed and no committed intermediate wires, checked coefficient by coefficient over 29‑bit limbs with their carries committed (Kishu's limb route);
  • relation, fingerprint: the same relation checked in a few PIOP instances over random primes, as BitZ does it, without the limbs and carries (BitZ, and Kishu's fingerprint route);
  • limbs: limb products as committed wires in another field (the 128‑bit and Goldilocks rows and Plonky3); or
  • bits: a Boolean circuit (the F2​ family and the binary groups).

The rule counts the first three (native and the two relation variants): such a configuration is dominated only by another such, while a limbs or bits configuration can be dominated by any. So the post‑quantum frontier always keeps the best native and relation points beside the cheaper other-field ones. How efficiently each realisation performs is what the transaction measure's application costs show.

The assumption works the same way: a configuration is dominated only by one that assumes no more. The hash-based families rest on a random oracle alone. Akita's and Kishu's rows rest on Module-SIS as well, so a Kishu row never removes a Flock or BitZ row from the post‑quantum frontier, however much cheaper it is. The Boolean-over-Akita row's security ledger is open, which is treated as making a stronger assumption.

Which measures

The second and third measures are chosen independently from the same eight. The defaults are the accumulation prover for the second and the transaction prover for the third, with the Ironwood recovery circuit as the transaction. The transaction prover may be both measures, each with its own application, so that two applications can be compared. The frontier is taken on proof bytes and both measures. The accumulation prover is what one fuse costs the prover beyond its own step: the merge circuits' commitments, which are prover commitment work, plus the fold's sum-checks over the accumulator, and for Kishu its merge's constraint PIOP.

Merge gates is offered since every family has an estimate of them. Accumulation atoms is kept because it is the more robust proxy for the lattice merge, whose gate count is estimated. For the hash-based families atoms say nothing, since their merge cost is the Merkle hashing. Decider work is the decider's verification cost: under ten milliseconds for the 64-bit and 128-bit lattice rows, the binary-field families and the hash-based deciders with BLAKE3 trees; 2.04 to 27.9 ms for Akita's three Pasta variants, Kishu and BitZ; 41.9 to 384 ms for Pedersen-IPA; and, with Poseidon trees, 5.33 to 33.8 ms for WHIR over Goldilocks and 25.3 to 167 ms for WHIR over Pasta. So it rarely decides a frontier, but it is there to check.

Transaction prover is the expected work to prove the application chosen below: the Ironwood recovery circuit, a transaction with four recovery inputs, the hardware wallet's part of the recovery statement on its own (the device's Hqk statement, or a leanSPHINCS verifier with either BLAKE2s or Keccak-256), a Zoodles transaction (two inputs and two outputs of a sketched protocol with no curve arithmetic) or one epoch of a Zoodles note's lineage, a number of Merkle path checks, or a Tachyon transaction of 2 to 16 tachyactions in Tachyon's own proof tree. For the post-quantum families the Tachyon transaction is Tachyon's own circuits, a pre-quantum protocol, proven in a post-quantum proof system, with their hashes under the page's policy. That is not a useful thing to deploy, which is why the Zoodles options exist, but it compares the proof systems on the same application. The recovery circuit recovers notes of the existing pool, so its nullifier stays Poseidon over Pasta. The application is costed in each family's own arithmetization, so it takes more steps where Pallas arithmetic must be emulated. The measure charges each step at the family's per-step commitment cost and one merge per step at the row's accumulation prover. The zero-knowledge rows also pay the masking work at the handoff to the public aggregator. The Transaction prover section below gives each application's cost in each arithmetization.

Parameter changes against design changes

The changes a configuration needs are the third requirement and work the same way, in the order of the table's Changes needed column: parameters only, then changes to Ragu's code, then changes to its design. A configuration is dominated only by one that needs no more, so a design change never removes a parameter-only configuration from the frontier, for example. The table's last column says whether a row is on its class's frontier or only on its family's. The per-family box collapses each family to its own frontier instead, so that a dominated family still shows its best configurations.

Rank

A step at rank r commits 2r coefficients: 2r−2 gates of four wires for the field arithmetizations, and 2r bits or digits for BitZ and Kishu, which alone go past rank 17.

For Pedersen-IPA, the circuit budget below limits the endoscalings per step and the binders at each rank, which makes rank a real trade-off. A larger circuit holds more endoscalings and fewer binders, which removes committed components and with them bytes and atoms, while the IPA grows by 128 bytes per rank and every remaining polynomial doubles. Rank 14 with the fixed circuits packed beats rank 13 on bytes, prover commitment work and atoms; ranks 15 and 16 buy bytes and atoms with prover commitment work.

For Akita the step circuits' witnesses open as one batch, so with Poseidon the rank moves bytes and atoms only through each circuit's own evaluation claim and the last circuit's unused capacity, a few hundred bytes across the range. With BLAKE3 the claims' absorption makes the rank decisive, as the Hashes section says. The more significant trade is the field choice: a smaller field buys fewer bytes and less prover commitment work at the cost of more atoms absorbed per merge.

Rank 12 has no Pedersen-IPA rows, since a 1,024-gate circuit holds no binder challenge, and no Akita rows under BLAKE3. Rank 17 helps Akita under BLAKE3, where fewer circuits absorb fewer claims: 14 to 30 percent off the merge prover, and 0.6 kbytes off the proof at the small fields, 3 kbytes for the Pasta variants.

The WHIR-type rows depend on the rank only through their circuit count, so they are shown at ranks 13 to 16.

The bit arithmetizations, BitZ and Kishu, whose steps commit 2rank bits or digits, go on to ranks 24 and 23, where one step holds the recovery circuit. Their merge is nearly a fixed cost, so the transaction measure falls with the rank until then, while the proof and the merge prover barely move; padding a step beyond the application would only cost. Rank 12 gives BitZ a slightly smaller proof and merge prover.

ARC against each scheme's own recursion

Every hash-based scheme appears twice, with ARC accumulation and, in a lighter shade of the same colour, with full recursion: the merge circuit verifies its two input proofs, each step emits a full proof, and the decider verifies one. The hash and the field are the same. The proofs differ, since the recursive decider verifies one stand-alone proof while the ARC decider's first round opens three oracles. So the recursive rows' proofs are a little over half the ARC rows' (212 kbytes against 376 kbytes for WHIR at rate 1/8 and rank 13).

For WHIR the recursion is about a wash on the prover at rate 1/8: the verifier's hashes per input match ARC's openings through the tree's levels (2,600 against 98 × 26 without grinding, and both fall with it). Its merge is two fifths larger. At rate 1/2 it saves a third of the prover and a twentieth of the merge, because the verifier's queries fall with the rate while ARC's openings grow with it. So with Poseidon trees the rate-1/2 recursive rows of WHIR over either field and of the limb hybrid dominate their ARC rows on every measure. Under BLAKE3 trees no ARC row is dominated by its family's recursive row, nor are the F2​ family's or BitZ's under either hash. FRI's verifier has twice WHIR's hashes, so its recursion costs about twice ARC.

Ligerito's verifier, under BitZ, opens 491 columns over its 5 levels at 100 bits, against ARC's 98 openings at rate 1/8. So its recursion is 7 times ARC's hashing (232 against 33 million witness bits at rate 1/8) and 7.4 times the prover, for a proof 23 percent smaller. The ARC row is the better one for BitZ on the prover and the merge.

The F2​ family's recursion verifies its own FRI-Binius proof, whose ring-switching verifier costs 2ℓ′⋅2κ field multiplications. So its merge is 100 million witness bits in the 192‑bit design, 145 million in the 191‑bit one, whose one-step ring switching costs the verifier 191 field multiplications per variable rather than 64, and 239 million in the 256‑bit one, against 33 million under ARC. The prover is 2.3 to 5.6 times the ARC row's, with the verifier's paths pruned as a multiproof. Its proof is a quarter smaller (158 kbytes against 214 kbytes at rate 1/8).

What the axes mean

Proof bytes

The compressed PCD proof. For Pedersen-IPA it is counted from Ragu's structs: the instance's commitments and scalars, two revdot reductions, two batches, and two IPAs with one round per bit of the rank; the checked-in configuration gives 7,908 bytes, which Ragu's wire format confirms (7,936 with its 28‑byte envelope). The two online polynomial commitments and six openings that every Ragu proof now carries are 448 of those bytes.

For Akita it is the planner's byte estimate for the decider's opening of one final group plus the separately committed groups, from the estimation runs, plus an instance of 128-byte commitments, two claims per group, and one claim per step circuit.

For WHIR with ARC it is the WHIR proof that decides the final accumulator. It is measured with the reference implementation over a 256‑bit field at 128‑bit security in the proven Johnson regime, at the batched witness size and the selected rate and grinding. Added to it are the two extra first-round trees of the decider's batched opening and the accumulator's roots and claims.

For the F2​ family it is the optimizer's proof as the F2​ family section describes, and for BitZ its Table 10 proof with the Zinc+ PIOP's, each with the extra trees under ARC.

For the binary-groups family it is Akita's measured opening of a binary source, extrapolated to the merge's bits.

Accumulation prover

The prover commitment work below plus the fold's own sum-checks. Akita's two norm and range sum-checks run over the accumulator in digits, at about five multiplications in the claim field per digit a pass (Pasta's field for the Pasta-claims variant, the 64‑bit field for Kishu). The accumulator is the batch group and the five stage groups. The batch is every step circuit's witness in one committed vector of circuits × 2rank coefficients, the merge's circuits and the application's, since the merge absorbs one image for it and the decider opens it at that length. A stage polynomial holds its values at the wires of its reserved gates and is zero elsewhere. Those zeros are structural and public, so what is committed and folded is the stage's support: 584 values in Ragu's native fuse at a header of 9. A lattice fuse's stages are taken to hold the same, a claim-field element each, which in Kishu is 26,000 committed bits. Akita's grouped opening admits groups of different dimensions [DBK+26, §5]. Kishu adds its measured Booleanity sum-check (438 ms for 227 bits on one core, 9.8 word multiplications per 64‑bit digit). The fold's own linear combination of the digit vectors costs one multiplication per digit. Since the batch is about the merge's size plus a circuit for the application, this measure is nearly flat in rank, like the commitments, until one circuit holds the merge, at rank 21 for Kishu, and doubles with each rank beyond, where the step is two circuits. It is the measure the transaction prover charges per merge.

The other rows add nothing: Pedersen-IPA's fuse is measured whole and its native folding, the batching of about 95 polynomials and a 100-point linear combination, is about one percent of it; the hash-based rows' ARC step already hashes the new accumulator; and the binary-groups row's measured opening includes its sum-checks.

Accumulator memory

What the prover holds between fuses, in bytes. A fuse holds the step's witness and one or two of them: two when both children are real proofs, one when the other child is the bootstrap proof. That is the fixed base case that Ragu's circuits recognise by its dummy suffix, as in a chain or in Tachyon's action steps.

For the lattice rows it is the folded digit vector, the accumulator's coefficients in digits (the batch group's circuits × 2rank and the stage groups' values, as the accumulation prover counts them), each digit stored at the width of its accumulator's norm bound. The certified ℓ2​ bound at the handoff is about 219 (the ledger of the zero-knowledge note, the zk note below), which bounds every entry, so 20 bits and a sign. Each fold multiplies the entries by up to 40, so an accumulator a level below the top needs five bits fewer. The measure is of the top level. The sum-checks expand a digit to an element of the commitment field on the fly, 8 bytes at 64 bits, 16 at 128, 32 at Pasta's modulus, which is computation, not storage.

Pedersen-IPA's is the uncompressed proof, every committed polynomial's 2rank Pasta coefficients, 26.5 Mbytes measured at rank 13 against 24.9 Mbytes counted.

The hash-based rows under ARC hold the accumulator's codeword, the witness over the rate in the field's elements, and its Merkle tree; under their own recursion only the previous proof. BitZ and the F2​ family hold the packed codeword with a tree of 256‑byte leaves, and the binary-groups row the packed bits.

At rank 17 Akita with Pasta claims holds about 29.4 Mbytes, Kishu at rank 21 about 11 Mbytes, and Pedersen-IPA at rank 13 25 Mbytes.

Peak fuse memory

What a fuse holds at its peak, in bytes. For the lattice rows it is three things. First, the two children's accumulators, with the output written over one of them as the linear combination is computed. Second, the fold's second-round sum-check table. The first round can stream over the packed digits, expanding each to a claim-field element as it goes, so the first table stored is the second round's: half the accumulator's digits at the claim field's width, 16 bytes for Kishu's extension, the 128‑bit field, and Goldilocks's extension, 32 at Pasta's modulus. Third, under zero knowledge, the mask: the accumulator's digits at the row's own coordinate width, 26 to 32 bits across the lattice rows, a masked coordinate stored compactly, with the response written over it. The new step's witness and the commitment's working set are small beside these. The other rows hold two accumulators, the output over one of them.

Kishu at rank 21 peaks at 70 Mbytes with zero knowledge and 56 Mbytes without; Akita with Pasta claims at rank 17 at 238 Mbytes; and Pedersen-IPA at rank 13 at 50 Mbytes, two uncompressed proofs.

Prover commitment work

Native 64‑bit word multiplications for one step's commitments, with every committed polynomial taken as dense. Pedersen over Pasta: a Pippenger multi-scalar multiplication costs about 255/rank mixed additions per coefficient, so the cost falls as 1/rank. The constant is calibrated to Ragu's measured fuse at the checked-in configuration: 1.46 s on one core of an Apple M4 Max for the step's circuit and its 91 recursion circuits with their stage polynomials, 96 commitments of 213 coefficients. That is about 5,600 word multiplications per coefficient at rank 13 and 5,200 at rank 14, over all of the step's polynomials. The earlier estimate, 11 field multiplications of 32 word multiplications per addition, was 24 percent higher; udon's AArch64 assembly, which Ragu does not enable, takes 13 percent off the measured time.

Ajtai by NTT, with the accumulation matrix shaped as Akita's catalog shapes its own, a module of a few rows over a ring of degree 512 or 1,024: per digit the module rank in pointwise ring products plus log2​(d)/2 for its share of the transform, at the modulus width, which is 32 word multiplications at 255 bits, 8 at 128, 2 at 64. The rank and degree are the cheapest that Akita's ℓ∞ estimator certifies at the floor for the row's bound and its accumulator's width (the security floor section). Without the mask every lattice row is at rank 1: 5.5 multiplications a digit at degree 512, or 6.0 at 1,024, which the widest accumulators at the 64‑bit modulus need. With 85 digits per Pasta coefficient, at a vector of 222 digits, that is about 15,000 per coefficient when the commitment modulus is Pasta, 940 when it is 64‑bit, 1,900 at a 128‑bit field, and 180 on Goldilocks, over every step circuit's witness. The cycle's endoscaling and binder polynomials do not exist in the lattice design. Folding and sum-check work is not included.

For WHIR with ARC it is the Reed–Solomon encoding by FFT over the witness divided by the rate, plus the Merkle trees of the witness and of the new accumulator. The trees are hashed by BLAKE3 at 200 word multiplications per compression by default, or under the arithmetic-hash option by Poseidon at about 35,000 per permutation over a 255‑bit field, since natively its matrix multiplications are full multiplications too. At rate 1/8 that is about 180,000 per coefficient with Poseidon and a few thousand with BLAKE3; but the circuits that a BLAKE3 merge needs multiply the committed witness, which is where the prover's cost then goes.

The F2​ family's prover is counted as the F2​ family section describes, a carry-less multiplication as one word multiplication, and BitZ's is its measured Table 10 prover. The binary-groups family's is the measured commit and open times per committed bit, taken for one thread, plus Flock's PIOP.

Accumulation atoms

An atom is one element of the merge circuit's native field. A configuration's accumulation atoms are the atoms that the merge circuit absorbs per fold, to derive the fold's challenges from the two proofs that it merges. The count stands in for the merge circuit's size: each absorbed atom costs hashing constraints, and the Pedersen coordinates also feed the point arithmetic. For Pedersen-IPA it is two atoms per commitment folded, the x and y coordinates, over the commitments of both instances. For Akita it is the sum-check messages of the range and norm checks, about 120 elements for two sum-checks of about 20 rounds with three elements each, counted as one atom each. Then each compressed commitment image: 128 bytes at the variant's atom width, which is 8 atoms at a 128‑bit field, 16 on Goldilocks, 4 on Pasta, and 6 for Pasta claims with 64‑bit commitment coordinates, three coordinates to an atom. Then one atom per step circuit's claim, and 18 more with zero knowledge. The folding arithmetic is not included, and for Pedersen-IPA neither is the endoscaling arithmetic, which is what a higher endoscaling count costs in gates.

For the hash-based families, with ARC or with their own recursion, the merge absorbs only the accumulators' or input proofs' roots and claims, about 40 atoms, which is why atoms are the wrong measure for them.

Merge gates

The gates synthesized across every circuit of one merge: measured for Pedersen-IPA, and estimated for Akita and for WHIR with ARC as the Circuit budget section describes. For the binary-field families, the binary-groups family and Kishu they are counted in AND gates, witness bits or digits, as their sections describe. It is the default third measure.

In the 2D view the marker's size follows the logarithm of the third measure over the plotted points, from 5 to 22 pixels, so the sizes read across any selection. The binary-field and BitZ families' witness-bit counts sit at the top of that range. Markers over 16 pixels carry a small contrasting cross at their centre, so that they can be read against the axes. The swatches in the families list are sized like each family's median plotted marker, up to 18 pixels, so the list carries the same cue.

Decider work

The decider's verification, in the same word-multiplication equivalents as the prover, at 3e9 per second of one core, which is also what the millisecond option assumes. Pedersen-IPA is modelled: the two IPAs each need a multi-scalar multiplication of 2rank points, plus a scalar multiplication per folded commitment to combine the instance, about 41.9 ms at rank 13.

Akita is measured: the paper's single-thread verifier takes 4.2 ms at the 128‑bit field and 3.9 ms on Goldilocks at 227 committed bits, growing by about 0.4 ms per doubling, so 2.59 to 3.08 ms at this witness size. The Pasta variants are taken at four times the 128‑bit figure, the ratio of word multiplications per field multiplication, since the verifier's work is sum-check arithmetic in the claim field: about 11.9 ms. With zero knowledge the final accumulator is at the ordinary length and the terminal's bounds are unchanged, so the verification is unchanged but for the few percent that one more step circuit's claim can cost.

The hash-based deciders are the WHIR verifier's hashes at the witness size, measured, at the variant's native permutation cost, plus about a million for the arithmetic, and in the ARC rows the decider's two extra first-round trees. At rate 1/8 and rank 13 that is 13.7 ms on Goldilocks and 65.6 ms with Poseidon over Pasta under ARC, and 7.68 and 34.5 ms under recursion, and about a millisecond in every case with BLAKE3 trees; FRI has 2.07 times the hashes.

The F2​ family's decider is the FRI-Binius verifier: the proof's authentication hashes over pruned paths and its leaf hashes at BLAKE3's native cost plus its field multiplications, 0.373 to 1.43 ms.

BitZ is its Table 10 verifier at the merge's bits, 2.42 ms at 225, scaled with the floor and, in the ARC rows, by the decider's two extra first-round trees, plus 2.00 ms for Zinc+'s PIOP.

The binary-groups family's decider is Akita's measured verifier for a binary source, at the paper's slope, 5.34 ms at the merge's bits.

Pedersen-IPA

Circuit budget

A step circuit at rank r holds 2r−2 gates and four times as many constraints, 2,048 and 8,192 at rank 13, and the gate limit binds first. The Pedersen-IPA figures are the internal circuits' synthesis counts pinned in Ragu's tests at rank 13 (tachyon-zcash/ragu 8109a41c). An endoscaling step of four points costs 1,995 gates, taken as 451 per point plus 191, since only the four-point step is pinned. A binder costs 2,032 to 2,048 gates for 2 of the 8 challenges, taken as 590 per challenge plus 860 of overhead; that split is derived, not measured.

The fixed circuits are hashes_1 (1,793 gates), hashes_2 (1,874), collapse (1,455, the two collapses merged), compute_v (1,948), bind_beta (1,889) and bind_endoscalar (940) on the native side, and collapse (1,598, with the export merged in), compute_v (1,504) and loading (566) on the nested side. Packing them into a larger rank's budget is first-fit decreasing on these counts, and merging circuits is a design change rather than a parameter.

Lattice-based families

Akita

Akita [DBK+26] is the lattice polynomial commitment scheme that these rows price. Its merge circuit is estimated, not measured. Its transcript hashing is priced at the selected hash: BLAKE3 at 14,900 gates per 64 bytes absorbed, the sum-check elements and the claims at the claim field's width and the six commitment images at 128 bytes each, or Poseidon absorbing four elements per 288-gate permutation, 72 gates per accumulation atom. Folding each child's 128-byte commitment image needs a modular reduction, taken as one gate per bit. The sum-check verifier's arithmetic is about 400 gates.

The step circuits are that total divided by the rank's budget, rounded up; each circuit's own evaluation claim is absorbed by the next merge, so the count is a fixed point. Under BLAKE3 a 16-byte claim costs about 3,700 gates to absorb and a 32-byte one 7,500, more than a rank-13 circuit holds, and the 32-byte one more than a rank-14 circuit. So rank 13 has no Akita rows under the default, nor rank 14 for the Pasta variants. Splitting a compression across circuits is taken as free, although a rank below 16 cannot hold one in a single circuit. Merge gates, in the hover text and the table, is the total over every circuit of one merge.

Kishu: BitZ over Akita (draft)

Kishu is the study's name for an arithmetization in BitZ's style over Akita's PCS. Every wire is committed as small digits under Akita's 64‑bit modulus, bits where the circuit needs bits and tribits for integer words; the constraints and the range check are sum-checks over that field's quadratic extension; and Pasta values enter as limbs or through a fingerprint rather than as claims in the Pasta field. Kishu is a Japanese dog breed, like Akita and Hachi. The arithmetization, its unit costs, and how it differs from Ragu's are on Kishu's Arithmetization. That page also gives the Booleanity check's two forms, the two routes for a Pasta multiplication, the merge's accounting under BLAKE3 and Poseidon, and the recovery circuit's count. The rows' figures are here.

Costs at rank 17

At rank 17 with BLAKE3 that is 1.2 million digits in 13 circuits, a proof of 74 kbytes, a merge prover of 3e7 word multiplications and a 2.37 ms decider in the sum-check form; with Poseidon 0.73 million digits, 74 kbytes and 1.7e7. Each circuit's claim costs 3,000 digits to absorb under BLAKE3 and 1,700 under Poseidon, so even a rank‑13 circuit of 8,192 digits holds its claim (268 circuits under BLAKE3). Kishu therefore has rows from rank 13 under both hashes, where the lattice rows under BLAKE3 start at 14.

Against the 64‑bit Akita variant, which commits every wire of a hash gate as a 255‑bit value, the merge prover is 190 times smaller under BLAKE3 (5.7e9 at rank 17) and 7.0 times under Poseidon. Under BLAKE3 the proof is smaller too (74 kbytes against 95 kbytes). So under conventional hashes Kishu dominates that variant on every measure but the merge's count, whose units differ; under Poseidon Kishu's proof is 10 kbytes smaller. Against BitZ at rank 17 the proof is 7.6 times smaller and the merge prover does 7.9 to 14 times less work.

Quang Dao thinks the prover here is likely overestimated: the commitment is priced at rows sized by the loose security analysis, with its grinding, and a tighter analysis would cut them. So the family's prover should be read as an upper bound. The plot's measures are the recursion's: the step's commitments, the accumulator's opening and the merge circuit, which every design pays and which can be estimated. Which application circuit to benchmark is hard to agree on, since it depends on the application; so the application enters the plot through the rank, and the transaction measure through its cost in digits.

Zero knowledge and status

The projection form of the Booleanity check reveals coordinates of the committed table, so no row that uses it has zero knowledge. The zero-knowledge rows use the sum-check form, masked as the zero-knowledge section describes.

The draft's certificates for the Booleanity check are conditional and not yet formalized.

LaBinius

LaBinius [OS26] is a lattice commitment whose modulus is decoupled from the constraint field: the commitment runs over a composite, NTT-friendly modulus, the evaluation claim lives in a binary extension field, and extraction avoids reduction modulo the commitment modulus by working over the number field. Its native opening is the amortised one, a square root of the witness in size, 314 kbytes at 218 elements and 3.0 Mbytes at 224; LaBRADOR compresses it to 75 to 88 kbytes at ten times the prover, with a verifier of 77 to 713 ms, all at 100 bits. For this study its importance is that it is a worked, implemented instance of the decoupled commitment modulus that the Pasta-claims-with-64‑bit-commitments variant assumes for Akita, with a soundness argument to adapt. It gives a decider only, with no accumulation or recursion layer, and Akita's own development has since replaced its root reduction with binary groups, which the next section plots.

Flock-style circuits over Akita's binary groups (experimental)

Akita's development branch commits a dense binary source as a group kind inside one ordinary grouped opening (LayerZero-Labs/akita#285, the binary feature; it replaces the LaBinius root reduction and nested commitment of its earlier PR #229). The bits are packed into 128‑bit carriers, the claim is a multilinear evaluation over a binary field, and the opening switches to the proof field inside. So the F2​ family's arithmetization, Boolean circuits with Flock's PIOP over F2128​, can commit with Akita instead of FRI-Binius and accumulate with Akita's fold instead of ARC.

The row prices that from the branch's own measurements of November 2026, at the P128 root; the P64 root is one to four percent smaller, with times within run-to-run noise. A binary-claim opening of 222 carriers, 229 bits, is 82,764 bytes. It is committed in 174 ms, opened in 648 ms and verified in 8.5 ms, on an M4 Max under load with the parallel feature on.

The merge is Akita's fold in a Boolean circuit, and that is our estimate. The transcript's 2.7 kbytes absorbed by BLAKE3 in blocks of 8,192 committed bits per compression, Flock's layout, native in a Boolean circuit under either hash policy, is 0.35 million gates; the fold of the twelve child images by a ternary challenge of weight 20, one adder bit per image bit per unit of weight, 0.27 million; one 128‑bit proof-field multiplication per sum-check element, 120 of them, 2.1 million, which dominates; and the two inputs' Flock PIOP verifiers, which the F2​ family's merge counts too, 1.5 million, for 4.1 million in all.

A multiplication is counted in AND gates with XOR free, the garbled-circuit cost model, by the cheapest of schoolbook, Karatsuba and Toom–Cook 3 at each width. A full adder is one AND, so schoolbook is about 2n2 at n bits; Karatsuba pays from about 20 bits and halves the count at 128; and Toom–Cook 3, with its exact division by three done bit-serially, takes a further two percent off. That is 16,400 AND gates at 128 bits, plus 800 for the reduction by 2128−275. That is 4.1 million AND gates in all, 8.1 times fewer than the F2​ family's ARC merge at rate 1/8, and not comparable with Pasta gates.

The proof is the measured opening extrapolated from 229 bits down to the merge's 221.3 at the planner's 563 bytes per doubling for the 128‑bit field, with the stage groups at that field's growth: 97 kbytes. The measured pair of sizes a doubling apart differ by 1.8 kbytes, which would make it 10 kbytes smaller, but one difference between single runs is not a slope.

The prover takes the measured commit time as the step's commitment, at ten times the measured time for one thread, since BitZ's benchmark gave four to five times on ten threads of this machine: 9.7 word multiplications per committed bit, plus Flock's PIOP at 2.3. The accumulation prover adds the fold's sum-checks over the accumulator, the merge's bits and the stage groups' values as bits, at the binary field's multiplication cost, as the lattice rows count them. The measured open time is the opening's, which the accumulation prover does not count for the lattice rows either. That is 5e7 for the merge's commitments, against 5.8e8 for the F2​ family's ARC step at rate 1/8, and against 6.6e8 for Akita over Goldilocks at rank 16 under BLAKE3. There the transcript's hashing in a Pasta circuit is what makes 51 circuits. So with conventional hashes a Boolean merge circuit over the lattice commitment is the cheapest merge prover on the page, since its hashing is native and its bits are cheap to commit. The row is on the post‑quantum frontier under the default.

The decider is the measured verifier at the paper's slope, 5.34 ms, where the F2​ family's is 0.373 ms. In the transaction measure a Pasta gate of the recovery circuit is about 1,650 AND gates here, since a Pallas multiplication in a Boolean circuit is about 120,000 of them. So the recovery circuit costs about 20,000 word multiplications per Pasta gate in this family, against 3,700 for Akita with Pasta claims over 64‑bit commitments. The family would suit an application that is a Boolean circuit in its own right, such as the batches of hashes that Flock targets; the recovery circuit, which is Pasta arithmetic, is not one.

Not modelled: zero knowledge, since the groups are not hiding; the 147‑bit floor; and the binary carrier field switch. The security ledger is open: the q24 Module-SIS certificate is not yet issued and the branch makes no security claim.

Hash-based families

These families rest on a random oracle alone: WHIR over Pasta, over Goldilocks and with the Pasta witness in 64‑bit limbs, a Plonky3-style FRI over Goldilocks, the Flock/Binius-style F2​ family, and BitZ, each with ARC accumulation and with its own recursion. What the hash-based route has that Akita does not is native Pasta arithmetic with no design change beyond the commitment scheme, and a prover whose hashing is cheap with a conventional hash. The default view prices that, and the Hashes section says what the recursion then costs.

The figures in this section are with Poseidon trees, the arithmetic-hash option; the Hashes section gives the BLAKE3 ones. WHIR with ARC accumulation is dominated by Akita on every measure, while the F2​ family and BitZ are the efficient end of the line; the subsections say how far.

WHIR and FRI

WHIR with ARC accumulation is dominated by Akita on every measure: with the grinding chosen per row its proofs are 202 kbytes to 1,530 kbytes, its prover is 32 to 2,300 times Pedersen-IPA's, and its merge is 0.68 to 6.4 million gates, 27 to 250 times Akita's.

The proof is the decider's. At the root nobody has yet combined the two child accumulators with the root's own witness, so the decider's proof opens those three oracles in its first round, each under its own Merkle root (Ulrich Haböck's point). A stand-alone WHIR proof of the same witness is 177 kbytes at rate 1/8 and rank 13. The two extra first rounds bring it to 376 kbytes, with their paths pruned as a multiproof, as the reference implementation already prunes its own.

The lower rates and the grinding, added after Ulrich Haböck's questions, take a third off its proof at rate 1/32 against rate 1/8 (261 kbytes against 376 kbytes at rank 13) and a third off its merge, at 2.5 times the encoding and hashing. The sizes are extrapolated from measurements at 217, 218 and 220. The growth per doubling is not uniform, since a folding round is added every two doublings. The three-doubling slope used here is about nine kbytes against five over the first doubling alone.

Goldilocks cuts its prover by about 5 times and its proof by a sixth, and grows its merge, since a Goldilocks Poseidon costs more gates per node. The limb hybrid is WHIR with the Pasta witness committed as four 64‑bit limbs per coefficient, tested over Goldilocks, with a Pasta merge circuit: the family list's "Pasta claims, 64‑bit limbs" rows. Unlike Akita's 64‑bit commitment variant it gains nothing: the Pasta merge circuit forces Pasta's hash on the trees, and four limbs per coefficient is more hashing, not less. WHIR over Pasta is dominated by Akita's Pasta variants, which is a like-for-like comparison.

The merge is estimated, as Akita's is. A hash commitment is not homomorphic, so Ragu's split accumulation does not apply; ARC accumulates Reed–Solomon proximity claims instead. Its verifier checks 2(λ−g)/log2​(1/ρ) Merkle openings per input at rate ρ with g bits of grinding in the query phase, in the proven, Johnson-bound regime. At λ=128 and 16 bits of grinding that is 224, 112, 75, 56, 45 and 38 at rates 1/2 to 1/64, and 256, 128 and 85 at 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 without grinding. The factor of two would go away only under the list-decoding conjectures refuted in late 2025.

Each opening is a path through the accumulator's tree over the witness divided by the rate, one hash per node, a BLAKE3 compression at 14,900 gates by default or a Poseidon permutation at 288 under the option. A merge has two inputs. The step circuits follow as for Akita, with the tree's depth growing with the batched witness, which is why the number of circuits is in the hundreds. WARP has the same opening count for Reed–Solomon codes and a linear-time prover only with linear-time codes, which does not help here, since the cost is the hashing rather than the encoding.

Verifying a WHIR proof in the circuit instead of accumulating, the other route, costs about the same hashing for a single oracle and more with the oracles of a real polynomial IOP. The proof of each step's growing witness is fed back into the next step.

The F2​ family

The binary-field, sum-check-based systems of 2025 and 2026, Flock [BRW26] and Binius64 on the FRI-Binius and Ligerito commitments, and Blaze on repeat-accumulate-accumulate codes, are the efficient end of the hash-based line. They are Boolean arithmetizations over F2​ with claims in F2128​, so they have no 2rank Pasta circuits and the rank filter does not apply to them; the Flock/Binius-style family is priced in its own terms. Its merge is ARC's openings as for the other hash-based variants, each Merkle node a BLAKE3 compression in a block of 213 committed bits, Flock's layout for a batch. So the merge is a Boolean witness of that many bits, 19 to 91 million from rate 1/64 to 1/2. Each input's PIOP verifier runs in the merge too, the zerocheck and the lincheck over the witness's variables and a sum-check per base matrix in place of the native verifier's own evaluation of the matrices: about 360.0 multiplications in the challenge field, 1.6 million AND gates by Karatsuba at rate 1/8, 4.9 percent of the merge. Its merge-gates figure is a count of AND gates that is not comparable with Pasta gates; bytes and prover commitment work are comparable.

Proof bytes come from Ulrich Haböck's FRI-Binius proof-size optimizer, in three designs that each row names: the witness packed into F2256​, which is also the field of the folding and sum-check challenges; packed into F264​ with the challenges drawn from its cubic extension F2192​, which is the field that the agreement bound sees, as Plonky3's FRI pairs a base field with an extension; or packed straight into F2191​, a prime-degree field with the trinomial x191+x9+1 and no subfields, which Ulrich Haböck suggested for its arithmetic. The proof is at 128 bits of security in the list-decoding regime up to the Johnson bound, with the largest list that the correlated-agreement bound allows (the simplified BCHKS25 bound; BCIKS20 for unique decoding). The codeword's length is counted in field elements, with the Guruswami–Sudan multiplicity, the selected grinding, the folding schedule chosen to minimise the compressed proof, and Merkle-cap multiproofs. Checked against the reference WHIR implementation at the same witness, field, regime and grinding, its query counts are within one to five of WHIR's and its proofs about a tenth smaller, from the optimised schedule. A 128‑bit field cannot reach 128 bits in any regime at these sizes, since the agreement term alone is about 100 bits, which is why FRI-Binius's published figures are at 100.

Ring switching [DP24, §1.3] packs 2κ bits into each element and assumes a power-of-two degree over F2​, which 192 and 191 are not. So the 192‑bit design packs into F264​ (κ=6) and needs the ring-switching sum-check restated over the tensor product of the two fields. The 191‑bit design lays the witness out as 191 columns, which the PIOP batches and the ring switching takes in one step of degree 191. Both are design changes that the paper does not write down. The first-round oracle is the packed witness and has the same bytes under any packing. So the designs differ in the later rounds' elements, 24 bytes against 32, and in the agreement margin, which sets the list: 220 to 221 at 256 bits, 28 to 29 at 192 and one less at 191, which costs them no query at these rates. So the 192‑ and 191‑bit proofs are about 5 percent smaller than the 256‑bit ones (214 kbytes and 214 kbytes against 224 kbytes at rate 1/8).

Under ARC the decider's first round opens three oracles, the two child accumulators and the root's witness, each under its own root, which the optimizer prices and schedules for.

Prover commitment work is counted in word multiplications, a 64‑bit carry-less multiplication as one. The PIOP is Flock's measured 82,100 BLAKE3 compressions per second on one core less its commitment (its Table 5: witness generation 5%, zero-check and lincheck 46%). The zero-check and lincheck, which run over F2128​, are scaled by half the challenge field's multiplication cost over F2128​'s: 4, 8 and 11 carry-less multiplications per product in 128, 192 and 256 bits, Karatsuba over the 64‑bit limbs with the limb reductions, and 7 in F2191​, whose one trinomial reduction is cheaper than the tower's six.

The commitment is counted operation by operation. The additive NTT of the first oracle, with a 32‑bit subfield twiddle per limb in the tower fields and a full-field twiddle in F2191​, which has no subfield to hold the evaluation domain, and its tree; the ring switching, two passes of a challenge-field element by each witness bit and a sum-check over the packed coefficients; and the folds, the folded trees and the BaseFold sum-check. These are counted in carry-less multiplications, BLAKE3 compressions and word XORs at an eighth each, and scaled to the FRI-Binius paper's single-threaded 144 ms commitment and 160 ms opening at 228 bits, rate 1/2, over F2128​ (its Table 2). The counts reproduce those at 1.1 and 1.7 times. An ARC step pays the NTT, two trees and the ring switching; a recursive step a full proof, and its merge verifies two, the field multiplications by Karatsuba.

So the prover grows with the inverse rate below 1/4, as the other hash-based rows do. With the grinding chosen per row it is 538 million word multiplications at its least, at rates 1/4 to 1/8, and 2.0 billion at rate 1/64 in the 192‑bit design. The 256‑bit one is up to 10 percent more, and the 191‑bit one from 4 percent less at rate 1/2 to 10 percent more at the lowest rates, where the NTT's full-field twiddles outweigh its cheaper reduction and half-size folds. Flock's whole measured pipeline is 150 million at this witness size and its own rate 1/2 over F2128​.

The decider's verifier is the proof's authentication hashes, with the paths pruned as a multiproof, and its leaf hashes at BLAKE3's native cost plus its field multiplications, 0.373 to 1.43 ms. Zero knowledge is modelled in two variants, a batched mask and a Zook-style one, which the zero-knowledge section below describes. It does not support the Pasta base field, so under the dominance rule it can be dominated by anything.

Its proofs under ARC are 135 kbytes to 550 kbytes from rate 1/64 to 1/2 in the 192‑bit design, with the three first-round trees, and under recursion 98 kbytes to 204 kbytes. The prover is least at rate 1/4, with rate 1/8 within a tenth of it, 538 million word multiplications, 20 times Akita over Goldilocks's with Poseidon and 0.81 of it with BLAKE3, whose proof is 73 kbytes to 77 kbytes. The merge is 19 to 91 million AND gates against Akita's 25 thousand Pasta gates with Poseidon, or 0.83 million with BLAKE3.

The price of the field is the application: Pasta arithmetic in a Boolean circuit, or in any small field, pays the embedding and simulation overhead that the small-field survey [Ska26, §5] quantifies, and the Ironwood recovery circuit is Pasta arithmetic. The transaction measure prices that at about 1,650 AND gates per Pasta gate.

BitZ

BitZ [BGK+26] removes that price. It is a hash-based commitment for multilinears over any finitely generated ring. The witness is bit-decomposed and committed packed over F2128​ with Flock's Ligerito. An evaluation claim over a ring R is lifted to the integers, through a random prime where R is large, and proved in the exponent of F2128​ by batched GKR grand products. So its cost is per committed bit and does not depend on R.

With the Universal Constraint Systems of Zinc+ [AGK+26] the application's Pasta arithmetic is integer relations, integer witnesses with ideal membership modulo p, projected to a random prime field for the PIOP. So the Ironwood recovery circuit stays Pasta arithmetic: a field multiplication is 255 bits of value and 255 of quotient, 510 committed bits, and a hash gate is one bit. So the recovery circuit is about 8.1 million bits, as the Transaction prover section counts. A step of rank r commits 2r bits of application witness, beside the Merkle hashing of the merge, which is most of its witness. The merge is a hybrid circuit: the Merkle hashing over F2​ as for the F2​ family, and the GKR and PIOP verifiers native over the binary extension and the projection field, about 1,800.0 products of committed elements, 451 thousand bits, 1.3 percent of the merge.

Its costs are the paper's Table 10: the PCS at 220 to 231 committed bits on one thread at 100 bits, interpolated at the merge's bits. The paper's own benchmark, run here on one thread, reproduces those bytes exactly at 225 to 228 and gives the scalings. On one thread this machine is 1.3 times the paper's and on ten threads it matches, ten threads giving four to five times the single-thread prover.

At 128 bits, which its implementation reaches only in the unique-decoding regime with fold grinding, the Ligerito part of the proof is 1.8 times the 100-bit one and the verifier 1.17 times, while the prover is unchanged. Rate 1/8 has 0.83 of the Ligerito bytes, and at the sizes the rows use its prover is the rate-1/2 one. The grand-product GKR, four fifths of the prover, does not depend on the rate, and the Ligerito phase's penalty for the lower rate appears only from 227 bits, where it costs 1.28 times in all. The two phases are priced separately. Rate 1/8 is the proof-size minimum: at rate 1/16, the lowest the implementation allows, the proof is 3% larger again and the prover 27% slower.

The unique-decoding regime is what the implementation certifies at 128 bits; at the Johnson bound it stops at 118 bits, its out-of-domain binding term with one sample. There the proof is 217 kbytes at 225 and rate 1/2, against 304 kbytes in the unique-decoding regime at 128 bits. The Ligerito part grows linearly with the bits (1.18 times from 100 to 118). So a Johnson-regime BitZ at 128 bits, which analysis in progress may reach, would be about 231 kbytes, a quarter less than the stand-alone figure under the rows. The rows keep the certified figures.

The prover is the grand-product GKR, 63 of Table 10's 80 ms at 225, with Ligerito the rest: as Quang Dao puts it, the prover with grand-product GKR is just really expensive. Zinc+'s PIOP is added from its Table 4: 1.6 times the PCS prover on the application's share, 2.00 ms of verifier, and 36 kbytes of proof.

At rank 13 and rate 1/8 with ARC it comes to 563 kbytes with the decider's three first-round trees, 2.4e8 word multiplications, a 33 million bit merge, and a 8.30 ms decider. Its Pasta arithmetic is one relation per multiplication, and no other hash-based family's row with native or relation Pasta arithmetic has both a smaller proof and a cheaper prover; Kishu, below, beats it on both. Akita's Pasta variants beat it on proof size, and its merge is a Boolean witness of the F2​ family's size.

BitZ's paper offers succinctness only; its zero-knowledge rows here are derived, as the zero-knowledge section says. Quang Dao notes that BitZ's arithmetization, the bit-decomposed witnesses with claims over any ring, might in future be combined with a lattice backend such as Akita.

Control knobs

The PCD header, the elements carried between proofs, is the application's choice and applies to every row alike: 2, 4 or Tachyon's 9 from the control. It is 9 whenever a Tachyon transaction or the recovery circuit is the application. The recovery statement's primary input, the anchor, rk, the nullifier and SigHash, is six or seven elements with the suffix, which a header of 2 or 4 does not hold. Each element is a packed Pasta field element for every scheme alike, 64 bytes in the proof for the left and right child's copies. The rows are priced without a header, and so are the figures in the text unless they say otherwise.

  • Pedersen-IPA: rank 13 to 16; endoscalings per step on both curves, 4 as checked in, up to what the rank's circuit holds; challenge binders, 4 as checked in, down to the fewest that bind the eight challenges at the rank; and the fixed circuits as today or packed into the rank's budget.
  • Akita: rank, and the field and modulus variant. The committed groups are five stages plus one batch of every step circuit's witness, and the number of step circuits follows from the merge circuit's gate estimate. Each step circuit's polynomial carries its own evaluation claim: one claim-field element in the proof, one atom per merge, and a few gates, which is why fewer, larger circuits help a little. The rank itself is set by the largest application step, not by the merge, which is spread over as many step circuits of that size as it needs. The opening sizes come from the planner's runs with groups of 214 coefficients, which overstates the cost of the small stage groups.
  • WHIR with ARC: rank; the code rate, from 1/2 to 1/64, which trades the prover's encoding and hashing against the number of openings and the proof size; the grinding, from the control above, one setting for every hash-based family or the best per row; and the field. Pasta is FFT friendly, so the witness, the trees and the merge circuit can all stay over it. Goldilocks puts everything over the 64‑bit field with the claims in its cubic extension, which 128‑bit security needs. Under the arithmetic-hash option it prices the merge with a width-12 Poseidon of rate 8 at about 480 gates and 7,200 word multiplications per permutation. The limb hybrid keeps a Pasta witness and merge circuit and commits each coefficient as four 64‑bit limbs tested over Goldilocks. So under that option its trees use Pasta's Poseidon over limbs packed three to an element. Under the default every variant's trees are BLAKE3. Basefold adds nothing here: its field-agnostic codes exist for fields that are not FFT friendly, and over Reed–Solomon codes it is subsumed by WHIR.
  • The F2​ family: the rate, the field design (256‑bit; 64‑bit packing with 192‑bit challenges; or 191‑bit, packed directly), the grinding, and under zero knowledge the variant; it has no rank, since its merge is a Boolean witness.
  • BitZ: rank 12 to 24, the grinding, and rate 1/2 or 1/8, the two its implementation measures.
  • Akita's binary groups: none. The row is the one measured configuration, the P128 root at the 128‑bit floor; the binary-groups section above says what it assumes.
  • Plonky3: the commitment layer of the STARK toolkit, univariate FRI over a small prime field with Poseidon2 hashing, priced over Goldilocks for comparability under the same ARC accumulation, with the same knobs. Its merge and prover match the Goldilocks WHIR variant, since ARC's openings and the Merkle trees do not depend on the low-degree test. Its decider proof is FRI's, 1.95 times WHIR's at matched field, rate and security, the ratio the WHIR paper measures. The ratio comes from the query counts, λlogd for FRI against λloglogd for WHIR. It is priced with the page's selected hash, BLAKE3 or Poseidon 1.1, rather than its default Poseidon2, and at 128 proven bits rather than the roughly 100 conjectured bits its deployments target.
  • Hashes in circuits: conventional only (BLAKE3), the default, or arithmetic allowed (Poseidon 1.1); the Hashes section below says what each changes.

The marker shape says what a configuration needs beyond its family. A circle needs parameter changes only. For Pedersen-IPA, rank, endoscalings per step and header size are constants in the code; for Akita, the 128‑bit field and Goldilocks are the paper's published parameter sets. A square needs more. For Pedersen-IPA that is a code change within the protocol: a binder that binds more than two challenges, or the fixed circuits merged. For Akita it is a design change: the Pasta variants need a modulus profile that Akita does not have, and the 64‑bit commitment variant a decoupled commitment modulus with its own soundness argument. The hash-based families are design changes throughout, with ARC or with their own recursion, since either replaces Ragu's split accumulation. The table says which.

Zero knowledge

Akita's mask

With the box ticked, as it is by default, the Akita configurations carry the masked witness of the zk note. The user's fold masks the accumulator witness by rejection sampling. That makes the one masked accumulator longer, 9 to 11 base-8 slices a coordinate across the lattice rows at their own accumulators, nine in the zk note's example at 222 digits. It also asks more of the accumulation matrix, since the zk note's extraction argument needs that matrix binding at the masked bound, and every accumulator is committed under it. On the coefficient ℓ∞ route that Akita's estimator certifies, the masked bound is the extraction's slack times the response's width, 14σ, with σ at each row's own accumulator: 18 to 24 bits above the unmasked bound, a fold's output. The table answers with one more rank, or the larger degree, or both: a factor of 1.0 to 1.33 on the commitment rate, 1.27 for Kishu's rows, whose rank 1 at degree 512 becomes rank 2 at 1,024. The zk note's own Euclidean route, where the rows grow as the square of the bound's log, puts the factor at 2.4 at its example; the ℓ∞ bound carries no N​, and a box in place of a ball, which is the difference (its §5.5).

The length stays at the zero-knowledge layer. The aggregator's first fold on a masked accumulator range-checks its nine digit slices and folds them back to the ordinary length with its other inputs, as every lattice fold decomposes and folds. So the merges above that layer and the decider's opening see witnesses of the usual size. The extra rank or degree stays with the accumulation matrix. Akita's internal levels and its terminal commit the final accumulator's ordinary witness under their own matrices and keep their bounds. The accumulation matrix's larger images enter the opening only as the first level's auxiliary digits, which are lower order.

On this page that factor of 1.0 to 1.33 falls on every step's prover commitment work. The merge priced here is one at the zero-knowledge layer, so it has three more rounds in each of its two sum-checks, 18 atoms. The opening and the decider's verification are unchanged but for one more circuit's claim where those atoms need it. Merges above the zero-knowledge layer pay the masked matrix's rate only, which the page does not show separately.

The accumulator memory measure counts the ordinary accumulator, stored at the handoff's norm bound. The masked accumulator is not in it, since it passes from the user to the aggregator rather than into any proof: as base-8 digit slices it is about 14 Mbytes, against 1.6 Mbytes for the ordinary accumulator's digits packed the same way. The first level's extra auxiliary digits are not modelled either. Three refinements would move these figures. A design that checks the masked fold under a matrix of its own would confine the extra rank or degree to that layer, worth at most the factor above, and proving the change of matrix is the obstacle (the zk note's §5.9). The slices come from base-8 digits, a Gaussian width of 48 times the norm of the challenge times the witness, and each row's accumulator, so Akita's eventual Pasta profile and its digit base change them. And the 18 atoms assume the first fold's range and norm checks run over the slices at once.

The zk note's §5.6 prices the mask's parameters on its Euclidean route, where every bit on the bound costs rows: weight-20 challenges in the accumulation matrix's ring of degree 512 against weight 32 in a smaller ring, and a Gaussian 48 times the norm wide against twelve or six, which trade rows for attempts, 2.7 at twelve and 7.5 at six against 1.3, with a masked accumulator of 12.6 Mbytes at six. On the ℓ∞ route the table moves in steps, and none of those widths crosses one here, so the width is a question of attempts, slices, and the response's size. The choice is explained below, and the zk note's §5.8 moves the attempts off the user's device.

Pedersen-IPA

Ragu's zero knowledge is in every fuse: each draws two fold randomizers and a batch mask a side, uniformly random polynomials of 2rank coefficients, folds the randomizers as claims of their own and batches the mask, and a rerandomization is two such fuses with the public bootstrap proof as the right child (tachyon-zcash/ragu at ef7668fb6bbf5df0b77e92760fdb52af726ebaf1; its book says the hiding argument is not yet audited). The Pedersen-IPA rows carry those commitments in every fuse, so the zero-knowledge rows are the plain rows.

WHIR and FRI

For the WHIR and FRI families the zero‑knowledge rows carry the overhead measured with Plonky3's HVZK-WHIR, which composes Zook [CFW26] into a hiding commitment. On one core over KoalaBear with a quintic extension, at rate 1/4 and 100 bits, the proof is 103.6 kbytes against 30.9 kbytes at 216 and 110.1 kbytes against 37.5 kbytes at 218: an additive 73 kbytes of mask spot checks. The prover takes 19 to 22 ms more, 15% at 218 and halving per doubling.

Zero knowledge is paid once per transaction, at the handoff from the user's private accumulation to the public aggregator. Under ARC the final accumulator carries the users' masked rows. So the rows add 73 kbytes, scaled with the floor, to the decider's proof and about 1,300 hash checks to its verifier. They put the masked prover's extra work, a few percent of one step at these sizes, in the transaction measure's fold. Under recursion the public merges and the decider's proof are of public data, so the rows equal the plain rows but for that fold.

That difference between the two accumulation styles is structural, not an artefact of the model. Recursion seals the private witness at the handoff, since the aggregator verifies the user's proof and discards it. Accumulation carries the users' oracles onward, as a random combination with everyone else's, until the decider opens the final accumulator, so the masks must still be there then. Akita's accumulation has the same shape, and more: the masked bound sizes the accumulation matrix that every step shares, which is why every Akita step pays the masked matrix's rate. Confining that rank to the zero-knowledge layer, with a second matrix and proven switches at the handoff, is worked through in the zk note's §5.9, where the switch's verifier cost is the obstacle. The mask symbols would be larger over Pasta's field, which is not applied, and whether ARC's accumulation preserves zero knowledge has not been examined, so the ARC merge is left unchanged.

The F2​ family

Flock and BitZ offer succinctness only, by their own papers; Flock expects zero knowledge could be added at low cost, through zero‑knowledge IOPPs or VEIL. The F2​ family's zero‑knowledge rows follow the zk option of Ulrich Haböck's optimizer as of 2026-11-12. A mask of the witness's size is added in the first round, which doubles that round's leaves and adds a 32-byte blinder to each. Later rounds carry neither, since the full-entropy mask, once combined with the witness in that round's sum-check, lets them run in the clear. A schedule with no reduction opens witness, mask and blinder at the query positions before the reveal. His revision of 2026-11-10 gave each leaf one mask row, which the page priced for a day; asked whether one row suffices, he confirmed that the mask must be as large as the witness and corrected the script.

The script does not model the prover, so the rows charge the mask's commitment, equal to the witness's, once per transaction in the fold. At rate 1/8 that is 35 kbytes more proof under ARC (249 kbytes against 214 kbytes) and two thirds of the row's prover in the fold. Under recursion the rows equal the plain rows but for that fold, as for WHIR. He adds that the leaf blinders could probably be dropped, since the mask has full entropy at leaf level, but keeps them because they make the analysis clean. Only the private witness needs masking, not the public polynomials, so the three first-round oracles that the ARC decider opens masked here are an upper bound. An earlier revision opened the mask in a separate round, which cost about 105 kbytes under ARC.

The second variant, labelled Zook-style and derived rather than measured, prices Zook's masks [CFW26] for FRI-Binius's own structure. The main oracle's zero‑knowledge encoding costs nothing in the proof, since its random coefficients fit the witness padding. Each folding round's sum-check variables get a group of four-coefficient masks, each with its own randomness, encoded at rate 1/256 and spot-checked 16 times through a pruned multiproof; the ring-switching claim's revealed element gets a mask of 2κ coefficients; and the terminal takes a full mask of its own size. FRI-Binius has no code switching and no out-of-domain samples, which are what make WHIR's masks large, since their message must hold the previous encoding's randomness, about a hundred coefficients. So its masks stay small, and as they belong to the proof rather than to the oracles, ARC's three trees do not multiply them. That gives about 30 kbytes more proof under ARC, with the masks' encoding in the fold, and nothing beyond the fold under recursion. Under ARC these rows cost a little more proof than the batched mask from rate 1/8 down (37 kbytes against 35 kbytes at 1/8) and less at rate 1/4, and a hundredth of the row's prover against two thirds.

Ulrich Haböck's view is that the full-entropy mask in a batching step before FRI is the way to randomize FRI-Binius. A more frugal mask would need the first rounds' sum-checks made zero-knowledge too, which is what these rows price. So they stay as the derived lower estimate. The one cross-check is that the same count reproduces Plonky3's measured 73 kbytes for WHIR. In the Zook-style rows the ring-switching mask is this page's design, not the paper's, and in both variants the ARC merge is left unchanged, as for WHIR.

Kishu

Kishu's sum-check rows carry Akita's mask as the lattice rows do: the masked matrix's rate on every step's digits, 18 more atoms in the zk-layer merge, and the user's masking fold at the handoff. The fold's rejection sampling runs over the accumulator's digits: the step's circuits × 2rank, the merge's and the application's, and the stages' 26,000. That is about the merge's size plus a circuit at every rank up to 21, where one circuit holds the merge, and two circuits beyond. For the recovery circuit Kishu's zero-knowledge optimum is rank 21, 0.220 s per note against 0.132 s without, 0.0379 s of it the sampling at 7.1 ns a sample. Its projection rows reveal coordinates and drop out, as the binary-groups family does, and as Pedersen-IPA drops out at 147 bits.

Where that cost goes. Of the 0.220 s, the fold is 0.0649 s: the sampling 0.0379 s, the masks' commitments under the masked matrix 0.0253 s and the handoff's merge 0.00164 s. The larger part is the steps and their merges: 2 at 76.4 ms, 0.153 s against 0.132 s without zero knowledge. What zero knowledge adds to them is the masked matrix, rank 2 at degree 1,024 in place of rank 1 at 512, which raises the commitment rate of every step and merge from 11.0 to 14.0 word multiplications a digit, and the zk-layer merge's atoms. The fold, the merge's worth of digits and the stages', and the masked rate together move the optimum down: with zero knowledge the best row is at rank 21 and takes 2 steps, where without it the best is rank 22 in a single step. The constraint PIOP is 29.9 ms.

Three things set it.

The sampler

The sampler is the one term that is pure implementation. The page's 7.1 ns a coordinate is measured on one core of an Apple M4 Max: AES-CTR randomness on the AES instructions, Box–Muller in doubles, Sheppard's correction, the tail check and the rounding, with 1.5 ns of it the randomness. With ChaCha20 in plain C the randomness is 7.7 ns and the whole path 14. The AVX Box–Muller sampler of Hülsing, Lange and Smeets [HLS18] takes 7.7 to 13 ns a coordinate on a 2014 core, measured without and with its ChaCha20 randomness. By Jeudy's theorem [Jeu26], a rounded Gaussian with Sheppard's correction, σ−1/(24σ), is a discrete Gaussian of width σ up to a Rényi divergence of 1+73aN/(33,177,600σ8) over N coordinates. At this width that is below 2−179, so the rejection-sampling argument carries over unchanged. What double precision cannot do is round exactly. A coordinate's error is its size times 2−53, which leaves about 2−25 of the coordinates undecided between two integers, one coordinate in 23 folds. That fraction is also the worst-case bound of [HLS18] on the divergence the error would leave. Refining those few coordinates in higher precision makes the rounding exact. The exact alternative, Karney's method [Kar16], costs about 300 ns a coordinate, measured at 290 to 470 ns by Du, Fan and Wei [DFW20]. With it the recovery would take 0.891 s at rank 19, and at 100 ns 0.479 s at rank 20.

The width of the mask

The Gaussian width α is the second. A wider mask needs fewer attempts, exp(12/α+1/(2α2)) of them. But σ=α∥cs∥ puts one more bit on the masked bound per doubling, and one more slice on the coordinates per three. On the ℓ∞ route the shared matrix answers the bound in steps rather than by a smooth rank: for Kishu's accumulator the table holds rank 2 at degree 1,024 from a width of 4 to 1,024, so the commitment rate stays 14.0 word multiplications a digit across the sweep, where the zk note's Euclidean route would charge about four percent per doubling (its §5.6). For the recovery circuit at the page's sampler:

Width αAttemptslog2​β∞​MatrixWord mults a digitBits a coordinateSlicesRecovery with zkRank
67.530.52 × 1,02414.02480.379 s20
122.731.52 × 1,02414.02590.261 s20
241.732.52 × 1,02414.02690.234 s20
