The time falls at each doubling across the table, by 3.4 percent from 48 to 96, since the matrix does not move and only the attempts do. Each attempt samples and commits the accumulator's digits, the merge's worth and the stages', so the fewer attempts of a wide mask are the whole gain within the measure. The transaction measure alone would therefore take the widest mask on its grid: every transaction-sized application's least is at the grid's top, 1,024, at every sampler rate (the device's statement alone, one compression, is left out, since its transaction is its merges). The minimum is shallow: the recovery circuit is within two percent of it from α = 150 up. What a wider mask costs is outside the measure: the coordinate width, 27 bits at 48 and 32 at 1,024, which sets the handed-over accumulator's size and the peak memory's mask; a tenth slice from 64, which the transfer and the aggregator's range checks pay; and the rate of the public merges, which does not move here. The page keeps 48, nine slices a coordinate and 1.3 attempts, within 9.9 percent of the measure's least for every transaction-sized application at the page's sampler. Nine slices hold up to a width of 54, where the attempts are 1.25, so a wider mask within nine slices is open.

The transaction's shape

The fold is paid once per transaction, so a transaction with four recovery inputs takes 0.128 s per note at rank 22. What does not help: the two-matrix design of the zk note's §5.9, whose switch costs an in-circuit opening; the bimodal variant, which needs a structure that hides a sign (the zk note's open point 9); and masking in blocks (its §5.7), which is open.

BitZ

BitZ's zero-knowledge rows are derived, since its paper offers succinctness only. Ligero's random row per Ligerito level puts one symbol in every opened column, so that the columns reveal nothing. That is 16 bytes per opened column in the decider's proof under ARC, about 23 kbytes at 128 bits with the three first-round trees, and nothing under recursion. Each sum-check gets a Libra-style mask polynomial: Flock's zero-check and lincheck, Zinc+'s PIOP and each layer of the GKR, a sum of univariates of degree three in each variable. The masks are committed as extra rows of the same Ligerito matrix under those random rows and opened with the witness, so that each sum-check runs over the masked polynomial. The masks are 1,600 field elements for a 225-bit witness, under a percent of the step, paid in the fold. Zook-style spot-checked mask oracles would cost about 100 kbytes here, one oracle per sum-check round over the GKR's 325 rounds, so they are not the choice. Whether ARC's accumulation preserves zero knowledge is not examined for BitZ either.

Security floor

Akita's catalog sizes every matrix so that the cheapest known attack on its Module-SIS instance costs at least 128 bits under the ADPS16 quantum core-SVP model, 20.265β for BKZ block size β. That puts every instance at block size 484 to 486. ARC's openings are counted at the same λ, and the F2​ family's optimizer runs at the floor, which shrinks its lists.

The accumulation matrix that the lattice rows commit under is sized the same way. For each row the model takes the cheapest module rank and ring degree, among the catalog's 512 and 1,024, that Akita's ℓ∞ estimator certifies at the floor for the row's bound, with the row's accumulator as the width, from the estimator's own width tables at the catalog's bound ladder, the bound rounded up to the ladder. The bound is the one the zk note's extraction argument needs: without the mask a fold's output, the two children at the challenge's weight and the step's own digits, and with the mask the response's width 14σ at the row's own accumulator, times the extraction's slack. The zero-knowledge section says what the mask adds; without it every row is at rank 1, as the catalog's own accumulation matrix is.

The 147‑bit floor, the page's default, re-plans Akita's catalog at that floor with Akita's own planner, so its openings are planned rather than scaled. It is 147 rather than 150 because Akita's rank-one compression maps certify at 147.3 bits at the catalog's geometry; the margin section below explains. The rank growth at that floor is applied to the inner images' share of the verification; the accumulation matrix that every step commits under is looked up in the floor's own table, as the margin section says. That share is the terminal's clear inner images at the shipped geometry, 1,344 coordinates whose bytes Module-SIS sets independently of the modulus. They are 33 percent of the opening at the 128-bit field, 35 on Goldilocks, 30 with 64-bit commitments, 26 with Pasta images at SIS size, and 42 with Pasta for everything, where they are 32-byte field elements. The verifier's work is taken to divide as the message does.

WHIR's proofs, measured over both fields, are 16 percent larger at 147 bits than at 128, and ARC's openings grow with the floor; the margin section below has both.

Pedersen-IPA over Pasta rests on the discrete logarithm in a group of order near 2254: about 126 classical bits by Pollard rho, and nothing against a quantum adversary. It is shown at the 128‑bit floor as the conventional pre‑quantum baseline, and under the arithmetic-hash option, since its circuits hash with Poseidon, so the page's defaults do not show it. It drops out at 147 bits, which it does not reach even classically.

The binary-groups row is shown at 128 bits only too, since its Module-SIS certificate is not yet issued.

The table's Assumption column names what each family rests on: the discrete logarithm on Pasta, Module-SIS with a random oracle, or a random oracle alone. It is one of the dominance test's requirements (Pasta and the scheme assumption). The next section says how much to trust the Module-SIS figures.

Grinding

The hash-based families can spend proof of work in the query phase: with g bits of grinding the queries need carry only λ−g bits. So ARC's openings per input fall to 2(λ−g)/log2​(1/ρ), and WHIR's own query counts fall in the same way. A fixed setting applies to every hash-based row at once, from none, 16, 20 and 24 bits. The default, best per row, gives each configuration the measured setting with the smallest prover, from a wider set of measurements, and the row's label says which.

Each row's proof size is measured at its setting with the reference implementation over both fields, rates 1/2 to 1/64, at 217, 218 and 220, with the growth per doubling taken over the three doublings. The earlier rows were measured at 20 bits while ARC's openings were counted without grinding, which this corrects. At rate 1/8 over the 256‑bit field the proof is 147 kbytes with no grinding, 130 kbytes at 16 bits, 126 kbytes at 20 and 121 kbytes at 24; at rate 1/32 it is 113 kbytes, 100 kbytes, 96 kbytes and 93 kbytes.

The prover pays 2g evaluations of the grinding hash per merge, taken as the family's own Merkle hash so that the merge circuit's check is one node per input. Each bit of grinding removes about one opening in a hundred, so about a percent of the circuits and of the prover, while the grinding's cost doubles. The prover is least where the two cross: at 17 to 19 bits for families with Poseidon trees (217 permutations are about 0.5 percent of a merge's prover at rate 1/8 and rank 13, 220 about 4 percent), and 12 to 18 bits for the F2​ family and BitZ. The minimum is shallow, within a percent from 16 to 20 bits.

With BLAKE3 trees, the default, the WHIR-type rows take 24 bits, the most measured, since 224 compressions are a small part of a merge spread over tens of thousands of circuits. The settings and the lower rates follow Ulrich Haböck's questions. The capacity regime, which would halve the openings again, is not offered, since its conjectures were refuted.

Hashes in circuits

Every hash that a merge circuit computes is one of two. The default is a conventional hash, BLAKE3, at 14,900 gates per 64-byte compression in a lookup-free R1CS over Pasta or Goldilocks and about 200 word multiplications natively. The option allows an arithmetic hash, Poseidon 1.1 over the circuit's own field: 288 gates per Pasta permutation absorbing four elements, about 480 for the width-12 Goldilocks one, and 35,000 or 7,200 word multiplications natively.

Arithmetic hashes deserve consideration on the merits: for large fields and the widths in question, none of the attacks on Poseidon 1.1 has come near an academic break, and Tachyon uses it. The reason to exclude them by default is future-proofing. For long-term storage that reason is decisive, though some of a proof system's hashes are ones that long-term storage does not depend on. If requiring conventional hashes causes only a small regression that does not affect deployability, they are the choice; the option shows what the arithmetic hash buys.

With the option the rows priced with Poseidon join the BLAKE3 ones rather than replace them. So a configuration that is better on some measure with the conventional hash stays on the plot, and each frontier takes the better of the two. Ragu's checked-in circuits use Poseidon 1.1, so the Pedersen-IPA rows exist only under the option.

What the default changes: Akita's merge absorbs its transcript, 4 to 9 kbytes, in 55 to 133 compressions instead of 146 to 218 Poseidon atoms. So the merge grows from about 25 thousand gates to 0.83 million at the 128‑bit field and on Goldilocks and 2.0 million for the Pasta variants, at rank 16. Each step circuit's evaluation claim then costs more to absorb than a rank-13 circuit holds, and a 32-byte claim more than a rank-14 circuit. So rank 13 has no Akita rows and rank 14 none for the Pasta variants, and the first ranks that hold them take 1,740 and 1,471 circuits.

At rank 16 the merge takes 51 circuits at the 128‑bit field and on Goldilocks and 122 for the Pasta variants, against 2 with Poseidon. So the merge prover is 26 times the Poseidon one at the 128‑bit field (6.3e9 against 2.5e8) and 28 times on Goldilocks (6.6e8 against 2.4e7), whose wider BLAKE3 accumulator at the 64‑bit modulus takes the matrix to degree 1,024 at this floor; 61 times for the Pasta variants, and 67 with 64‑bit commitments, for the same reason. The proof grows by 4 to 4 kbytes at the small fields and by 10 to 11 kbytes with Pasta claims, from the per-circuit claims, and the atoms by 49 to 120. The per-step commitment cost and the decider are unchanged. The lever that would recover most of this is to aggregate the step circuits' claims before absorption, a design change.

For the WHIR-type rows every Merkle node becomes a BLAKE3 compression, so the merge grows 35 to 61 times (1.3 to 76 million gates for WHIR over Pasta at rate 1/8 and rank 13, 614 to 37,225 circuits). The prover grows 1.3 to 2.0 times for WHIR over either field and for FRI, since the trees get cheap but the circuits multiply. The limb hybrid's prover instead falls 2.2 times, since its Poseidon over limbs is dear natively. The decider's verification falls 17 to 83 times, to a few milliseconds; the proofs grow by a sixth with the larger batched witness, and the best grinding moves to 24 bits.

The F2​ family, BitZ and the binary-groups family hash with BLAKE3 already and do not change, so under the default their comparison with Akita is like for like. At rate 1/8 the F2​ family's ARC row proves a merge in 5.8e8 word multiplications for a proof of 214 kbytes, against Akita over Goldilocks at rank 16 with 6.6e8 and 77 kbytes. Its merge is 19 to 91 million AND gates against Akita's 0.83 million Pasta gates, which are not the same unit.

Transaction prover

The transaction prover measure prices a whole transaction rather than one merge, so that the cost of zero knowledge can be seen against the steps it belongs to. The transaction proves an application chosen above: the Ironwood recovery circuit; a transaction with four recovery inputs, which is four of the circuit under one zero-knowledge handoff; or a number of Merkle path checks of 32 levels and the leaf; or the hardware wallet's part of the recovery statement on its own, or a Zoodles transaction of two inputs and two outputs, both priced in the application subsection; the Tachyon transactions have the next section.

The application is costed component by component in each family's own arithmetization, under the selected hash policy. The family's steps are then as many as hold it, rounded up, since a transaction smaller than a step pays a whole step. A step circuit of rank r commits 2r coefficients, which is 2r−2 gates of four wires for the field arithmetizations, 2r bits or digits for BitZ and Kishu, and 222 AND gates for the Boolean families, which have no rank. Each step is committed at the family's per-step cost, which is the row's prover divided by its circuits, and there are as many merges at the row's accumulation prover, the merge's commitments and the fold's sum-checks. Kishu's step is a slot of whole circuits that the merge and the application share: the merge's digits and the step's transcript take the first part, and the application's nodes fill the rest, at least half a circuit, as many as fit. Its digits are charged at their own number, at the row's cost per digit, since a zero digit costs the Ajtai hash and the range sum-check nothing, while the fold's sum-checks and the mask run over the whole slot.

The application in each arithmetization

Off Pasta the recovery circuit's curve arithmetic is emulated, in the ways the requirements section lists: about 14,500 multiplications in Pallas's base field, in five fixed-base and one variable-base scalar multiplication with complete additions, 160 Sinsemilla chunk additions and the nullifier's Poseidon. Its seven BLAKE2b compressions, the chunks' generator selections and its Merkle path are bit operations and cost about the same gates in any prime field. Over Pasta the circuit is 570,000 gates with a Poseidon path and 1.05 million with a BLAKE3 one. Over Goldilocks a multiplication is about 1,100 gates, with nine 29‑bit limbs and no lookups, so the circuit is 16.5 and 17.0 million gates; at a 128‑bit field, with 61‑bit limbs, about 700 gates give 10.7 and 11.2 million.

In a Boolean circuit a multiplication is about 120,000 AND gates, the 255‑bit product by Karatsuba and Toom–Cook and a Montgomery reduction by a prime of no special form. A 64‑bit addition is 64 ANDs and an XOR is free, so the hashes cost half their Pasta gates. The circuit is 1.73 billion AND gates, the multiplications nearly all of it.

In BitZ's integer arithmetization a multiplication is 510 committed bits, the value and the quotient, checked as one integer relation, while a hash gate is one bit and a 64‑bit addition 65, so the circuit is 8.1 million bits. In Kishu over Akita the claims are in one fixed field, so a multiplication is either 374 digits by the limb route or 170 by the fingerprint route, which pays per step instead. The circuit is 6.1 million or 3.2 million digits, plus its constraint PIOP, which the Kishu section prices. The bit arithmetizations hash the path with BLAKE3 under either policy, since Poseidon over Pallas's field would cost them 240 multiplications a node.

A Merkle path check is 33 nodes: 9,500 Pasta gates, or 15,600 Goldilocks or 128‑bit-field gates, with Poseidon in the field; 492,000 gates in any prime field with BLAKE3; 240,000 AND gates; or 370,000 bits or digits. So the recovery circuit's hashes are what make the bit arithmetizations cheap, a path-heavy application makes them cheaper still, and the Boolean families pay for every Pallas multiplication.

Further applications price the hardware wallet's part of the Recovery Statement, which ZIP 2005's Option A proves on the device that holds the quantum spending key, the host proving the rest ([ZIP-2005], Key storage options). The device's own statement, qk=Hqk(qsk) with the linking commitment left out, is one BLAKE3 compression: 14,900 gates in any prime field, 7,170 AND gates, or 11,200 bits or digits. If the device instead signs SigHash with leanSPHINCS, the stateless hash-based signature of post-quantum Ethereum [EIP-8288] [Lit26], the host proves the verifier with the signature and the public key as witnesses. For [Wam26]'s pruned key that is 262 Keccak-f permutations, or 298 compressions of BLAKE2s or of BLAKE3, plus the 4,276-byte signature as input bits. XOR is not free in a digit arithmetization, so a Keccak-f permutation is 92,200 committed bits where a BLAKE2s compression is 15,800 and a BLAKE3 compression 11,000. What the wallet proves, what it hands over, and what the two routes cost on the device and in the transaction are the subject of the Spend authorization section.

Zoodles is a sketch of a spend protocol with no curve arithmetic at all, named for the pasta-free noodle, and priced as a transaction of two inputs and two outputs. It keeps Tachyon's architecture (the next section): the same tree of spend, output, merge, and fee steps, and a note's membership and unspentness attested by a background lineage over the chain's anchors rather than by a Merkle path in the spend. The published tachygrams are roots of set polynomials that the merges multiply at the challenge: a spend's two epoch nullifiers, an output's commitment and padding, and the fee step's change commitment. In Tachyon the set polynomials are Pedersen vector commitments and the bridge hash is a Pedersen hash onto Pallas. Here they are the proof system's own committed vectors with evaluation claims, and the bridge hash is a BLAKE3 hash of the commitment, computed natively. A root then costs one multiplication in a 256-bit extension of the claim field, and an opening one more claim, absorbed by the merge above and folded by a few multiplications: 3,020 Kishu digits. The curve goes. Amounts are range-checked and summed in the PCD headers in place of value commitments and the binding signature. Spend authorization is chosen per input, usually the same for all: a Sprout-like preimage check: the payment key is the BLAKE3 hash of the nullifier key and the quantum key, and the quantum key is the BLAKE3 hash of the quantum spending key, as ZIP 2005 derives it, so a spend proves two compressions where Tachyon's spend step derives the payment key alone; or a leanSPHINCS signature at the pruned key, with BLAKE3, BLAKE2s, or Keccak, over a transaction digest, verified in the circuit with the public key as a witness, since the zero-knowledge fold hides the key and no re-randomized signature is needed. The preimage check needs no digest: it is proved inside the spend step, which the tree binds to the rest of the transaction, directly and through the PCD headers. A signature is made outside the proof, so its message must bind the transaction's effecting data: each spend's two nullifiers, each output's commitment, the change commitment, the fee, and the epoch, 235 bytes or 4 compressions. The digest is a PCD header value: each spend verifies its signature over it, and the fee step recomputes it from the nullifiers and commitments that its children's headers carry, which a small transaction's headers hold. At the rank the signature transaction favours that hashing is under a tenth of one step; the signature verification is the expensive part. The fee step fixes the fee last and hashes the change note, the maximum-fee note's value less the fee, as Tachyon's does. Every hash is BLAKE3. The tree's 12 nodes hash 16 compressions in all, with 12 roots and 15 openings. The lineage's steps run in the background and are not in the transaction, as Tachyon's are not; one epoch of them is priced below.

In Kishu the preimage transaction is 259,000 digits and the signature one with BLAKE3 7.03 million, the two verifiers being most of it. With zero knowledge Kishu proves the preimage transaction in 0.0506 s on one core at rank 18 and the BLAKE3 signature one in 0.299 s at rank 22, so the preimage route is under a quarter of the signature route; without zero knowledge they are 0.0272 and 0.163 s. In the other families, preimage then BLAKE3 signature: BitZ with zero knowledge 0.0817 and 0.168 s; Boolean over Akita 0.0767 and 0.153 s at its 128‑bit floor; Flock 0.195 and 0.389 s; and Akita over Goldilocks with a Poseidon tree 0.287 and 9.02 s. Tachyon's own four tachyactions, with their curve arithmetic, take 0.143 s in Kishu with zero knowledge and 0.105 without, and 0.298 s in BitZ, so Zoodles by preimage costs less in each, 35 percent of Tachyon with zero knowledge. A simpler Zoodles that proves a 32-level Merkle path in each spend, opening the note there and deriving one nullifier, with no set polynomials, is 920,000 digits by preimage and 0.0772 s with zero knowledge, 54 percent of Tachyon, and still costs less than Tachyon in Kishu and BitZ; by leanSPHINCS with BLAKE3 it is 0.308 s. Its two paths are most of its digits. The Pasta-native families reverse the order: with Pedersen-IPA under the arithmetic-hash option Tachyon is 8.44 s and the Merkle variant 50.6, since a path's hashes cost a prime field more than the curve does. Flock takes 10.5 s on Tachyon, 54 times its Zoodles figure, due to the Pallas multiplications in a Boolean circuit.

The lineage's own cost is the wallet's witness update, one step per note per epoch of 4,096 blocks, about 1.2 days at 25-second blocks: the shape of Tachyon's unspent lift. The step proves that the note's nullifier for the epoch is not among the epoch's published tachygrams. Tachyon attests that with a bucket, one residue profile's share of the epoch's tachygrams. The share is partitioned by whether x+Rj​ is a square at successive discriminants, down to at most 8,192 members (the size of its online polynomial slot), and folded as a set polynomial that the step opens at the nullifier. Over Pedersen a commitment folds in one scalar multiplication. Over digits the bucket's tachygrams would enter the wallet's accumulator element by element, 2.10 million bits or digits, and set its rank. Set polynomials are the right tool over Pedersen and a dear one over digits, so Zoodles uses a sorted Merkle tree instead. The builder sorts the epoch's tachygrams once for everyone and hashes consecutive pairs into the leaves, so an exclusion proof is one leaf, the nullifier's two neighbours, with its path. The step derives the epoch's nullifier, hashes the leaf, proves the path, compares the nullifier with both neighbours, and range-checks the epoch. For a tree of 1,048,576 tachygrams that is 22 hashes, 247,000 Kishu digits, under a sixth of the bucket's. The tree's size is a choice, 256 tachygrams a block over the epoch, between the bucket's 213 and a busy chain's 224. Each doubling adds one hash to the step, and a shorter epoch adds steps a day. Kishu takes 0.0273 s a note an epoch on one core at rank 18, without zero knowledge, since the lineage never leaves the wallet. BitZ takes 0.0812 s, Flock 0.195 s, Akita over Goldilocks 0.0319 s, and Pedersen-IPA 6.33 s at its 128‑bit floor. The lineage's best rank is the spend's own, so the spend that consumes it inherits a rank it would choose anyway: Zoodles by preimage at rank 18 is 0.0506 s with zero knowledge.

The masking fold

For Akita's zero-knowledge rows the user's masking fold is added. It is the expected rejection-sampling attempts, 1.3 at the page's Gaussian width, plus the handoff's merge. That merge is the small one that the zk note's §5.8 deferral leaves the user. It derives the challenge from the mask's commitments and its evaluations at the claims' points, checks the commitment identity on those images, and folds the claims, in whole step circuits of the rank. The decomposition of the response and the range and norm proofs are the aggregator's first fold's, which the zero-knowledge-layer merge that the accumulation prover prices already carries. Each attempt is a commitment of a mask the size of the accumulator under the masked accumulation matrix, and as many Gaussian samples at about 7.1 nanoseconds a sample as a rounded Gaussian with exact rounding, 21 word multiplications at the page's rate. The sampling does not depend on the modulus. The fold is paid once per transaction whatever it proves. The mask covers the user chain's last accumulator, the merge's circuits × 2rank digits and the stages'. The device's statement is the exception: the wallet hands over a bare leaf without a fuse of its own, so its mask covers the leaf's 2rank digits alone, and the merge that folds the leaf is the host's. The hash-based zero-knowledge rows likewise put their masked prover's extra work in the fold, once per transaction; under recursion that is their only zero-knowledge cost, since the public merges and the decider's proof are of public data. Pedersen-IPA's blinding is free. This is total work, not latency: the zk note's §5.8 precomputes candidate masks in idle time and defers the decomposition to the aggregator, which leaves the device a sparse ring product and the transfer of the masked witness. An Orchard-style action has the recovery circuit's mix, with one path check and no BLAKE2b.

Results

For the recovery circuit, per note on one core, Kishu takes 0.132 s at rank 22, in 1 merges by the fingerprint route, and BitZ with ARC 0.167 s at rank 23, where one step holds the circuit; Akita with Pasta claims over 64‑bit commitments takes about 25.1 s at rank 17 with Poseidon, nearly all of it the fold's sum-checks over the accumulator's 85 digits per coefficient in Pasta's field, and 1,920 s at rank 17 under the default BLAKE3 trees; Akita over Goldilocks 16.1 s with Poseidon; and Pedersen-IPA, at its 128‑bit floor and the checked-in configuration, about 6.76 minutes, in 278 steps of rank 13, or 1.90 minutes at rank 17 with 72 endoscalings per step.

With zero knowledge Kishu's best is 0.220 s at rank 21 by the fingerprint route, and Akita with Pasta claims about 25.7 s at rank 17. BitZ stays at 0.168 s, having no rejection-sampling fold, with 23 kbytes more proof.

Tachyon transactions

The transaction options of 2, 4, 8 or 16 tachyactions, half spends and half outputs, keep Tachyon's own proof tree (tachyon-zcash/tachyon 73031f7, Stamp::prove). A spend is two steps, an output a seed and a step, each action after the first a merge, then the fee step and Ragu's rerandomization: 3s + 3o + 2 nodes for s spends and o outputs. The rerandomization is two fuses in Ragu as it is, each with the public bootstrap proof as the right child; Tachyon's pinned Ragu did it in one.

The page re-packs that tree for each rank's step size: a node larger than a step takes whole steps and its remainder joins the rest, which fill steps first-fit decreasing, and each rerandomization fuse is its own step. So at rank 13 over Pasta no two action circuits share a step and the merge rides with the fee step, 7 steps for two tachyactions against Tachyon's 8. At rank 15 every circuit of two tachyactions fits one step beside the two rerandomization fuses.

The nodes' circuits were measured through Ragu's synthesis analysis on Tachyon's steps at its header size of 9: 1,630 and 1,649 gates for a spend's two steps, 1,467 and 1,351 for an output's, 17 for an action merge and 1,934 for the fee step, in Pasta gates with Poseidon, all within rank 13's 2,048. In the other arithmetizations the transaction is Tachyon's circuits as they are, a pre-quantum protocol proven in a post-quantum proof system: the Poseidon permutations, 192 gates each in Ragu's gate model, are hashed under the page's policy; the fixed-base multiplications' window selections cost the bits' four monomials; and the window additions and the openings of staged values at ζ are Pallas multiplications. The remaining gates are the scalars' bit checks, the canonicity and range comparisons and the step's glue, priced as bit operations, one gate or committed bit each, which understates any among them that multiply field elements. So a node that is one step over Pasta is 6 to 8 steps of rank 17 over Goldilocks with Poseidon and 5 to 7 Boolean steps, which is where the range of step counts comes from. Pricing the remaining gates as multiplications too would give 27 to 39 Goldilocks steps.

Per-note steps that run in the background are not counted; a Zoodles note's lineage step, their counterpart, is an application of its own. A Tachyon transaction also needs Tachyon's header of nine elements, so while one is selected every row is shown at that header. The recovery circuit's options do the same, since its primary input needs six or seven elements.

On one core at the default floor, Pedersen-IPA at its own 128‑bit floor, two tachyactions take: with Pedersen-IPA at the checked-in configuration 7 fuses, 10.2 s, where Tachyon's own tree of 8 fuses is 11.7 s, and at rank 15 with 16 endoscalings per step 3 fuses, 6.33 s; Akita with Pasta claims over 64‑bit commitments 3.08 s at rank 15 with Poseidon; BitZ 0.265 s at rank 20; Kishu 0.0868 s at rank 19 with Poseidon by the limbs route; Akita over Goldilocks 1.15 s in 36 steps with Poseidon; and the F2​ family 6.03 s in 31. With zero knowledge Akita with Pasta claims takes 4.33 s and Kishu 0.117 s, and BitZ is unchanged.

Sixteen tachyactions take: Pedersen-IPA 51.1 s in 35 steps at rank 13, or 19.0 s in 9 steps at rank 15; Akita with Pasta claims 5.58 s; BitZ 0.363 s; Kishu 0.175 s; Goldilocks 7.17 s.

For scale, Orchard's Halo 2 prover, measured on the same machine with assembly, takes 1.88 s for two actions and about 14 s for sixteen on one thread. So Tachyon on Pedersen-IPA is 3.6 to 5.4 times Orchard per action on one core, and about three times that again on all cores in the current implementation, which has had less attention to parallelization of the fuse.

How much to trust the Module-SIS parameters

Akita's advantage over the hash-based route rests on Module-SIS, where that route rests on a random oracle alone and Pedersen-IPA on the discrete logarithm. This section states what the parameters assume and where the uncertainty sits.

The sizing rule

Every matrix in Akita's catalog is sized so that the cheapest known attack on its Module-SIS instance costs at least 2128 operations under the quantum core-SVP model of [ADPS16]. That model charges 20.265β for lattice reduction with BKZ block size β and ignores the polynomial factors.

The block size that reaches a given root Hermite factor is taken from the BKZ 2.0 analysis of [CN11]. Every instance in the catalog lands at block size 484 to 486, in lattices of dimension 2,000 to 4,800. The catalog's own security check reports 128.26 bits on each.

A cross-check with the maintained lattice estimator [LE] agrees on the ranks. The estimator is maintained; the paper that introduced it, [APS15], is not, and its authors say so in a 2019 note. The estimator costs BKZ as 8n calls to an SVP oracle of the block size, with sieving per [BDGL16] classically and per [LMvdP15] and [Laa16] quantumly. It follows [ADPS16] for the primal attack, as [AGVW17] established, and leaves out the dimensions for free of [Duc18] and [ADH+19]. The same block size under other models:

Cost modelBits at β = 484, the 128‑bit floorAt β = 556, the 147‑bit floorSource
classical sieving, 20.292β141162[BDGL16]
quantum sieving, 20.265β, the floors used128147[Laa16], as adopted in [ADPS16]
"paranoid" lower bound, 20.2075β100115[ADPS16]

For calibration, ML-DSA [FIPS204], the standardized Dilithium, sizes its SIS instances at block sizes of about 423, 638 and 909 for its three security levels [Dil21]. These parameters therefore sit between its levels 2 and 3 on the same model.

Where the uncertainty sits

Three places, in decreasing order of concern.

  • Proof-level slack, not the assumption. Lattice schemes have slipped before by sizing for honest norms rather than the extractor's. Akita sizes for the extractor's collision bound, which is why the masked variant needs rank 340 against 143. But the knowledge-soundness proof in the quantum random-oracle model is still in progress. And the decoupled commitment modulus has no soundness argument yet beyond the LaBinius analogue. A gap of that kind moves parameters by a lot, not by twenty bits.
  • The instantiation is unusual. Ring dimension 64 with 128‑bit or 255‑bit moduli, compression rings of dimension 8 and 4, and norm bounds up to 248 are far from the regime of the standardized schemes. No attack exploits module structure beyond constant factors. Module-SIS has a worst-case reduction [LS15], and the quantum attacks on ideal lattices [CDW17] need principal ideals, which modules of rank 64 and more do not present. But there is less cryptanalytic attention on this corner, and the ℓ∞​ bounds take their own estimator route.
  • The cost model. Core-SVP is already a lower-bound style model. Refinements since 2016, such as the dimensions for free of [Duc18], have moved concrete estimates by ten to twenty bits either way. The disputed dual-attack improvements of [MATZOV22], reassessed in [DP23], concern LWE rather than SIS, which is attacked through the primal route. A 147‑bit quantum floor is 162 classical bits, and the paranoid model still gives 115; at 128 bits, 141 and 100.

Against the other assumptions

The hash-based route's assumption is weaker in the good sense: a random oracle and collision resistance only. Its soundness risk is concentrated in the proximity-gap conjectures, which is exactly where the 2025 refutations landed. The proven Johnson regime is therefore where that route is priced here.

Pedersen-IPA rests on the discrete logarithm on Pasta, about 126 classical bits and nothing against a quantum adversary. So the fair statement is that Akita dominates on efficiency while adding one assumption whose concrete hardness is estimated rather than proven. That assumption has SIS studied since [Ajt96], Module-SIS since [LS15], and standardization behind it.

A margin

The 147‑bit floor, the page's default, puts the block size at 556 against the 128‑bit floor's 484 to 486. The security-floor option above re-plans Akita's catalog at the higher floor with Akita's own planner. Its single security policy is retargeted to 147 bits, its runtime width tables are regenerated by its estimator at that floor, and its six rank-one compression cells are re-sized from them. So the openings at 147 bits are planned, not scaled.

The floor is 147 rather than 150 because the compression chain is built from rank-one maps. At the catalog's geometry its first map, at ring dimension 16 and width 4,096, certifies at 147.3 bits. A 150-bit floor allows that map a width of 3,806, so the chain would need rank-two maps, or two maps where it has one, and either doubles the compressed images at every level.

The accumulation matrix agrees about where the floor's cost begins. Of the 196 lattice rows shown at both floors, 18 take a larger matrix at 147 bits than at 128: BLAKE3 rows of the Akita variants, whose merges' many circuits make wide accumulators, and 8 Kishu rows at rank 23 without zero knowledge, the widest accumulators of all. Kishu's rows keep their matrices from 147 to 150 bits. At 150 bits 2 more would move, the unmasked matrix of the Pasta-claims rows with 64‑bit commitments, from degree 512 to 1,024.

The planner does not give the prover's rows term or the verifier's inner-image share. For those the model takes the weakest Module-SIS instance of each of the 115 schedules in the shipped catalog's security report and, for each, the smallest module rank that covers the instance's width at both floors. With the catalog's own mix of moduli the ranks sum to 121 at 128 bits and to 150 at 147 bits, a factor of 1.24, with 29 instances moving up a rank. Over a 64‑bit modulus, where the ranks are higher to begin with, the sums are 185 and 211, a factor of 1.14, with 26 moving. Over Pallas the instances sit at the width cap at both floors but one: the sums are 117 and 118, a factor of 1.01, with 1 moving.

Where the floor binds, the maximum secure widths shrink several-fold. At 147 bits the median shrink, over the cells where neither width is at the estimator's search cap and the width falls, is a factor of 2 to 3 at ring dimensions up to 32, 4 to 10 at 64, 4 to 13 at 128 and 256, and 6 to 15 at 512 and above, with the 32-bit modulus at the low end of each range. The few cells at the largest dimensions whose 147-bit width is still finite shrink about 36-fold.

The hash-based rows at the higher floor

The floor moves the hash-based rows too, through λ alone and independently of any lattice instance. WHIR's proofs, measured with the reference implementation at 217 over both fields at rates 1/2 to 1/8, are 16 percent larger at 147 bits than at 128, and its verifier's hashes 12 percent more; ARC's openings per input, 2(λ−g)/log2​(1/ρ), grow by 15 percent.

Kishu

Kishu is the draft lattice route in the comparison: Ragu’s proof-carrying-data arrangement and split accumulation, arithmetization ideas from BitZ, and Akita as the polynomial commitment scheme. Each wire is committed as small digits under Akita’s 64-bit modulus, bits where the circuit needs bits and tribits, digits of three bits, for integer words. The constraints and the range check are sum-checks over that field’s quadratic extension, and Pasta values enter as 32-bit limbs or through a fingerprint rather than as claims in the Pasta field. The name follows the naming convention of Japanese dog breeds used by Akita and its predecessor Hachi, with a nod to the “u” from Ragu.

Kishu has not been implemented. Kishu’s Arithmetization gives the arithmetization and its differences from Ragu’s, with a rough cost model. The frontier page’s Kishu section prices it beside the competing schemes, but many details remain to be filled in.

Zero Knowledge for a Lattice Accumulation Step shows how the user’s fold of an Akita accumulator is made zero-knowledge by rejection sampling, the masking fold that Kishu’s zero-knowledge rows pay for. Kishu’s Soundness Obligations states what has to be proved for Kishu: Akita’s own knowledge soundness at its 64-bit profile, the Booleanity check, and a limb lemma.

The idea of combining Akita and BitZ came from their designers. We would particularly like to thank Quang Dao (Akita), Albert Garreta (BitZ), and Tal Derei (Tachyon Project), for fruitful discussions with Daira-Emma Hopwood at the Cambridge PQC workshop. The performance and security modelling, the suggestion to use them in Zcash, and the name Kishu came from Daira-Emma. Ulrich Haböck made suggestions on performance modelling that influenced the design.

Kishu’s arithmetization

Kishu is a proof-carrying-data scheme in Ragu’s shape. An application is a tree of nodes. Each node is a circuit that takes the public headers of its input nodes, checks whatever the application needs, and publishes a header of its own. The scheme attests that every node in the tree was satisfied, so that a verifier checks one proof for the whole tree. What differs from Ragu is what a node’s circuit is written over. This page describes a node’s circuit as its writer sees it, then the pieces Kishu is built from, the costs the frontier page prices it by, and the differences from Ragu’s arithmetization. Every figure is the model’s (Regenerating the Study’s Numbers).

Kishu as a Proof-Carrying-Data scheme

A node’s circuit has:

  • a witness, the values its prover knows;
  • a header, the values the node publishes, which the scheme carries to the node above; and
  • the headers of its input nodes, which the scheme attests.

The circuit’s writer states constraints over these three, and the scheme guarantees that a proof of the node exists only if the constraints hold and the input nodes were proved. A transaction is formed from a tree of nodes, as in Tachyon: a node for each spend and each output, nodes that combine them, and a node that fixes the fee, with the root’s proof the transaction’s. (For efficiency we distinguish nodes in the PCD graph from steps of the accumulation scheme, discussed below: a step is what the prover commits at once, and several nodes can share one.)

The arithmetization

Let q be a fixed prime; q=264−59 for the modelled parameters. Write ⟨x,y⟩=xTy for the inner product of two column vectors over the field Fq​. A matrix in Fqr×c​ has r rows and c columns, so that premultiplying by it takes a column vector in Fqc​ to one in Fqr​.

Consider a Kishu circuit over Fq​ with m constraints. The public inputs, padded to length m with zeros, form the instance vector v∈Fqm​. A witness is a vector of N small integers, w∈ZN, read as elements of Fq​. The circuit fixes each position’s alphabet: a bit, in {0,1}; a dibit, in {−2,−1,0,1}; or a tribit, in {−4,…,3}, Akita’s own balanced base-8 digit. The entries are called digits.

The circuit is defined by, for each constraint index j,

  • fixed (typically sparse) coefficient matrices Aj​,Bj​∈Fqtj​×N​, where tj​≥0; and
  • a fixed coefficient row vector cj​∈Fq1×N​.

The constraint at index j requires this equality in Fq​:

⟨Aj​w,Bj​w⟩+cj​w=vj​.

In words: each row of Aj​ and the matching row of Bj​ give two linear combinations of the digits in Fq​, which are multiplied. These products are added up over the tj​ rows, together with one more linear combination of the digits given by cj​. The total must equal the constraint’s entry of v. So a constraint is a polynomial of degree at most two in the digits, with no constant term, set equal to zero or to a public input. Leaving out the constant term loses no generality: if one public input is the constant 1 and one witness bit is constrained to equal it, a constant term in any constraint is a multiple of that bit.

That every entry of w lies in its alphabet is enforced for the whole witness at once by a range check, not by a constraint per digit. For the bit positions it is the Booleanity check.

Relation to R1CS

This is a generalization of R1CS over Fq​ with several products allowed in one constraint. The digits’ range constraints are implicit.

Relation to CCS

CCS [STW23] writes a whole constraint system as one vector equation over z=(w,1,x), the witness, the constant 1, and the public inputs:

i∑​ci​⋅◯j∈Si​​Mj​z=0.

The Mj​ are fixed matrices, each Si​ is a multiset of their indices of size at most the degree d, ◯ is the Hadamard (entrywise) product between vectors, and the ci​ are constants.

Read row by row at degree two, that is the form above. Each Si​ then names one or two matrices. For a pair, their rows at a constraint, the first scaled by ci​, are a row of Aj​ and the matching row of Bj​. The single matrices, scaled, sum to cj​. A tj​ that varies with j is the same as padding Aj​ and Bj​ with zero rows up to a fixed number.

CCS puts the constant 1 and the public inputs inside z, where they can enter the products. Here the witness is small digits and the public inputs stand on the right-hand side. A constant or an input that a product needs is first copied into witness digits by a linear constraint. CCS allows degrees above two; here the degree is two.

Relation to Universal Constraint Systems

Universal Constraint Systems [AGK+26] are the constraint systems of Zinc+, over polynomial rings in general. Over the integers they are the constraint systems of Zinc [GWHD25]: CCS on a witness of bounded integers, with lifted moduli. The relations are proved by projecting them to a random prime field for the PIOP, so that one constraint system serves any moduli. That is what makes them universal. BitZ [BGK+26] proves integer polynomial constraints the same way.

Kishu keeps the shape of the constraints and the small integers as witness, but evaluates the constraints in Fq​ itself. Its fingerprint route is Zinc’s method, the relations checked in instances over random primes; its limb route is not, holding the relations over the integers by keeping the left-hand side of each constraint within a range no larger than q.

Relation to Ragu

Ragu’s arithmetization is the constraint system of Bootle et al. [BCC+16], over the Pallas base field and with a fourth wire added to each gate. A circuit of n gates has four wires a gate, each gate enforcing ai​bi​=ci​ and ci​di​=0, and 4n linear constraints, each a fixed linear combination of all the wires equal to an instance value (Ragu’s arithmetization chapter).

Kishu’s wires are digits of one to three bits rather than field elements, so a boolean value needs no gate. Constraints are over the 64-bit Fq​, not a Pallas-sized field. Its constraints are not gates of a fixed shape with a fixed number of linear constraints, but quadratic constraints with any number of products each, as above. In both Ragu and Kishu, the public inputs enter as instance values.

Writing circuits

The writer pays per digit of witness, per product, and a little per nonzero coefficient — less for a small one, such as the powers of two that assemble a word from its digits. A sum-check could take higher degrees at a cost per degree, but the model charges degree two. Fusing Keccak’s steps into cubic constraints was found not to pay; a term of higher degree costs an intermediate witness value instead.

A digit’s width is the writer’s choice, position by position. A value that is a factor of a product needs the width the product needs: a bit, in the hashes. A value that enters constraints only through linear combinations is written in tribits. That is any integer word: a limb, a quotient, a carry, an amount, or an element of Fq​. A dibit or a bit takes the remainder if the width is not a multiple of three. The commitment, the fold, and the mask cost the same per digit at any of these widths. The range check costs one product a bit, two a dibit, and four a tribit, by Akita’s paired predicate. So a tribit holds three bits for a little over a third of their cost.

A word of ℓ<64 bits is a linear combination of its digits plus a constant, which costs nothing to form. The constant offsets the balanced digits. Bit vectors of any fixed length can be represented directly, as can elements of Fq​ (non-canonically, in 22 digits). A range check is free: a value held in digits of ℓ bits in all is below 2ℓ by construction.

Since a word is a linear combination in certified digits, a relation holds over the integers whenever it holds in Fq​, provided that its two sides, as integers, both lie in a range no larger than q, so that they cannot differ by a multiple of q. That is how integer arithmetic is written. Adding a value in [0,u] to one in [0,v] is safe whenever u+v<q, for example. A 32-bit addition is a+b=s+232c with the sum and the carry committed, and a comparison is a subtraction’s carry. A multiplication of two words costs one product term; a constant costs by its nonzeros.

Arithmetic in a prime field other than Fq​, such as Pasta’s base field, is a relation with a committed quotient. Each multiplication carries a quotient and carries, which Kishu commits as tribits. An R1CS emulation of the same arithmetic pays mostly for the boolean constraints on the bits of those values, which Kishu’s digits do not need, so in Kishu’s arithmetization it is expensive but not prohibitively so.

Bit operations are a term each: XOR is z=x+y−2xy and AND is z=xy; rotations and shifts are wiring and cost nothing. A result needs committing only where it is a factor of a later product. A result used linearly, as an addend or as a hash’s output, stays an expression inside the constraint that uses it. In a chain of XORs every other word is committed, each certified against both XORs’ inputs at once at two terms a bit. A third XOR in a chain would need degree three. Bitwise operations keep bits. A dibit XOR is degree two only with a committed quotient digit, which is pinned only by committing the reduced result. Tribits have no degree-two XOR at all. So a BLAKE3 compression is 11,000 bits of witness and 11,120 terms, a multiplication in Fq​ is one term over 64-bit operands, and a Pasta multiplication is 170 or 374 digits by one of two routes. The circuits that suit Kishu are the hash-heavy ones.

A step is one or more circuits of 2rank digits, the rank chosen for the application between 13 and 24. The merge’s digits take the first part of the step, and the application’s nodes fill the rest, as many as fit, as the Zoodles page’s packing shows. Zero knowledge asks nothing of the circuit’s writer: the scheme hides the witness, and no randomizer or blinding wire is needed. Not available: lookup arguments, which the study does not model.

What Kishu is made of

Kishu is an arithmetization in BitZ’s style over Akita’s commitment scheme.

Akita is a lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme, secure under the Module-SIS assumption: it commits to a vector of small integers, its digits, by an Ajtai hash over a ring with a 64-bit modulus (its own digits are balanced base-8 digits, a few bits each), and it accumulates many such commitments into one by folding, so that a proof-carrying-data scheme can defer the expensive opening to the end.

BitZ is a hash-based commitment scheme whose witnesses are bit-decomposed: it commits the bits and proves an evaluation claim over any ring by lifting it to the integers.

Kishu takes BitZ’s view of the witness as small integers and the constraint style of Zinc+’s universal constraint systems. It commits the witness with Akita: bits where the circuit needs bits as factors, and Akita’s own base-8 digits for integer words. So the committed vector is the witness itself, the range check certifies it, and Akita’s accumulation replaces BitZ’s hashing-heavy proofs. A digit is therefore the unit in which this study counts a circuit’s size. The two arithmetizations are not the same. BitZ states integer relations and proves them by projecting to random prime fields. Kishu evaluates its constraints in Fq​, Akita’s commitment modulus. It reaches the integers either by keeping each constraint’s sides within a range no larger than q, the limb route, or by random-prime instances as BitZ does, the fingerprint route.

The piece that such a combination needs is a range check over the lattice’s own prime field, to certify that every digit lies in its alphabet. For the wider digits that is Akita’s own paired predicate, a sum-check of degree b/2 for an alphabet of b values. For the bits it is a Booleanity check, and an internal research draft of September 2026, provisional and unreviewed, supplies one. The committed table’s bits are certified by one unweighted quadratic identity plus an integer norm bound, which a structured random projection supplies by revealing 160 coordinates. So BitZ’s exponent-lift GKR, 79% of its prover, is not needed. The draft measures the reduction alone, single-threaded at 227 bits over 264−59. The projection prover takes 113 ms against 438 ms for the optimized conventional Booleanity sum-check, with verifiers of 0.85 and 0.023 ms and payloads of 2.6 kbytes and 1.7 kbytes. Neither includes the commitment opening or hiding. The projection form reveals coordinates of the committed table, so the rows that use it have no zero knowledge; the zero-knowledge rows use the sum-check form. The draft’s certificates are conditional and not yet formalized; Kishu’s Soundness Obligations states what has to be proved.

Beneath the step interface, Kishu accumulates as Ragu does: each step’s proof is folded into an accumulator rather than verified, and a step’s circuit is accompanied by a circuit that verifies the fold of its input proofs’ accumulators, the merge, written in the same arithmetization. The sections below price the arithmetization’s units, the merge, and the application circuits in them.

Digits and constraints

Kishu commits its digits over Akita’s 64-bit modulus, plus the range check. For a bit that is the Booleanity check at 2.5 or 9.8 word multiplications. A dibit or a tribit costs one or three products more at the same rate, charged with the application’s constraints. A step commits 2rank digits. Its constraints are charged as well as its digits: the constraint PIOP, a sum-check over the committed table, costs about 9.8 word multiplications per product term of a constraint, the measured rate of the Booleanity sum-check. A nonzero coefficient of a linear combination costs 2 for a small constant or 4 for a field constant, the combinations being over word entries. This is charged for the application’s constraints and the merge’s alike, and the PIOP’s transcript is absorbed and its verifier run in the merge above.

Its claims live in the 64-bit field itself, Akita’s commitment modulus, and the verifier recomposes each Pasta value from 32-bit limbs proved as linear claims in the same sum-check. So Kishu does not use the decoupled commitment, and its soundness rests on Akita’s own at the 64-bit profile and on the draft’s Booleanity certificate. Its opening proof and decider are priced on the Goldilocks variant’s plan and measurement, the same profile, at Kishu’s digit count.

Pasta multiplication by two routes

Akita’s claims are in one fixed field, so a Pasta multiplication a⋅b=k⋅p+r over committed digits cannot be checked modulo that field alone: the prover could choose r. Kishu’s rows therefore come in two routes, each a row. By the limb route the relation is checked coefficient by coefficient over 29-bit limbs, which are linear in the digits and cost nothing to commit. That is 17 constraints of up to nine product terms each, bounded below half the modulus so that they hold over the integers, with a committed carry of 34 bits each. A multiplication is then 374 digits and 98 product terms. By the fingerprint route the relation is one constraint in each of 3 PIOP instances over random 52-bit primes, as BitZ checks it, at 170 digits. The price is per step that has multiplications, so a step of hashes alone pays nothing and the routes tie on the path applications. Each instance’s evaluation claim becomes about 2rank​ integer column sums by BitZ’s tensor split, each exact as one claim in the 64-bit field and committed as a word of 61 bits, 21 digits. That is 91,300 digits a step at rank 21, with three more transcripts for the merge above. So the recovery circuit is 6.1 million digits by the limb route and 3.2 million by the fingerprint route. Its constraint PIOPs take 0.0134 and 0.00553 s on one core. The range checks of its tribits take 0.0509 and 0.0244 s more, beyond the one product a digit that every digit pays.

The merge

Kishu’s merge is Akita’s, costed in digits. A committed bit is one digit, so a BLAKE3 compression of the transcript is 11,000 digits and the images’ reductions one per bit. The BLAKE3 accounting is its seven rounds of eight G functions. Every word of a G function is used once as a factor, in an XOR, and once linearly, in an addition, and only a factor needs committing:

  • each 32-bit addition is one relation a+b=s+232c over word entries, with the 32 sum bits and the carry committed, two bits of carry where there are three addends;
  • of each chain of two XORs in a G function, the first’s word is left uncommitted: its bits are the expressions x+y−2xy inside the addition that takes the word, 32 terms there;
  • the second’s word is committed, each bit certified against both XORs’ inputs at two terms;
  • rotations are free, being wiring; and
  • the finalisation’s XORs are expressions in whatever consumes the output, except the four words that are the next compression’s factors in its first round, which are committed at one term a bit.

That is 11,000 digits, 11,120 constraints and 37,504 nonzeros a compression. The same accounting at 64 bits, each addition in two halves since a 64-bit sum can wrap modulo q, gives BLAKE2b 38,272 digits and 37,760 constraints. Under BLAKE3 every transcript element the prover supplies is first checked to be below the modulus, since a 64-bit decomposition is canonical only there, about 22 digits a word.

The merge’s arithmetic is over the 64-bit field and its quadratic extension, which is the PIOP’s own field. As in BitZ, the constraint PIOP runs over the ring itself, and only the final linear claim is proved on the bits. So a multiplication there is one constraint, with no bit decomposition and no quotient. But every wire is committed as tribits: 22 digits for a field element and 44 for a product in the extension. So the sum-check’s arithmetic is 400 such products, each circuit’s claim 4 and the Booleanity sum-check’s verifier about 3,000; the projection verifier scans 3.1 million sampled coefficients, a digit each. The transcript’s elements and each circuit’s claim are elements of the extension, 16 bytes, and the Booleanity sum-check’s own transcript is absorbed with them.

Under the Poseidon option the transcript is hashed by Poseidon over the 64-bit field at width 12 and rate 8 with the x3 S-box: 276 multiplications a permutation at 22 digits each. That is 54% of BLAKE3’s committed digits per absorbed byte, fewer because Poseidon’s wires are tribits where BLAKE3’s are bits. A permutation is 276 constraints with 13,800 nonzeros of field constants, where a BLAKE3 compression is 11,120 with 37,504 of small ones, and these are charged at the rates above. Per 64 bytes absorbed, commitments and constraints together, BLAKE3 costs 430,000 word multiplications and Poseidon 350,000, within 20% of each other, which many modelling choices could sway either way. So both hashes are kept as variants of Kishu on the frontier page, each a family of its own in the list and the plot. The BLAKE3 rows appear under either hash option and the Poseidon rows under the arithmetic-hash option, and the frontier decides between them.

The recovery circuit

The Ironwood recovery circuit itself is hash-heavy: its expensive parts are seven BLAKE2b-512 compressions (the cost section of [ZIP-2005]; beside two Sinsemilla commitments, two full-width Pallas scalar multiplications, a Merkle path, and a BLAKE3 compression in the quantum-key signature). In Kishu a bit-oriented hash is one bit per wire against many Pasta gates per round in the others, and the integer arithmetic simulates Fp​ without a bit decomposition per operation, with range checks free. A Sinsemilla chunk selects one of 1,024 generators by ten bits, each coordinate a fixed linear form in the subset products of the bits. Only a product that is a factor of another is committed: the 52 subsets within each half of the bits. The 961 subsets spanning both halves are terms of the two coordinate constraints. So a chunk is 222 digits with its coordinates. Costed component by component in this arithmetization, with a committed bit at one digit and a multiplication at 374 digits by the limb route or 170 by the fingerprint route, the recovery circuit is 6.1 million or 3.2 million digits. In Pasta arithmetic it is 570,000 gates. The frontier page’s transaction measure uses those counts together with the constraint PIOP’s work.

A rough cost model

The unit costs above, gathered. A digit is one committed bit, dibit, or tribit. A term is one product term of a constraint, or one product of the range check beyond the first. The word multiplications are native 64-bit ones on the prover.

WhatDigitsTermsProver work
a committed digit10, 1, or 3 for a bit, a dibit, or a tribit11.0 word multiplications to commit, 14.0 under zero knowledge
a Pasta value, as tribits85935 word multiplications to commit
a constraint term19.8 word multiplications; a nonzero 2 or 4
an XOR of two 32-bit words, committed3232, or 64 when the next XOR’s word is left uncommitted
an XOR of two 32-bit words, uncommitted032, inside the constraint that consumes it
a 32-bit addition33, or 34 with three addends1
a field element of Fq​; a product in E22; 441
a BLAKE3 compression11,00011,120
a Poseidon permutation over Fq​276 × 22276
a Pasta multiplication170 by fingerprint, 374 by limbs3 or 98the fingerprint route’s column sums per step besides

a step2rankits digits’ commitment and its constraints’ PIOP
the merge of one step1.2 million at rank 17, in a step of 13 circuits; the merge within one circuit, beside the application’s, from rank 21as a step’s

A transaction’s prover work is then its steps’ commitments and PIOPs, a merge for each step, the fold’s sum-checks over the accumulator, and the final opening. The frontier page’s axes Accumulation prover, Prover commitment work, and Transaction prover say how each is counted, and its Rank section how the step size is chosen. Zero knowledge adds the masked accumulation matrix’s rate to every digit and the masking fold once per transaction, as Zero Knowledge for a Lattice Accumulation Step describes.

Differences from Ragu

Relation to Ragu above gives the differences in the arithmetization itself. Beyond it, Ragu commits a step’s trace as one structured polynomial of degree below 4n, by Pedersen, and checks the gates and constraints together by one revdot identity at random points, sound by Schwartz–Zippel in the field. A step of rank r commits 2r coefficients, so 2r−2 gates: at rank 13, Ragu’s production rank, 2,048 gates, which every one of Tachyon’s circuits fits. Kishu differs in these ways:

  • A value’s digits cost less than a coefficient. Ragu’s gate costs about one Pallas multiplication of Pedersen work per wire, about 5,600 word multiplications a coefficient at rank 13. Kishu’s digit costs 11.0 to commit, so a Pasta value’s 85 tribits cost 935, well under one coefficient.
  • Constraints are a sum-check, not a gate identity. Ragu’s constraints are the fixed gate shape and linear combinations, checked by one polynomial identity over the field. Kishu’s are a sum-check PIOP over the committed table, as in BitZ and Zinc+’s universal constraint systems, with integer relations projected to the 64-bit field or to random primes. A constraint is charged by its product terms and nonzeros rather than by gates.
  • Hashes are cheap and Pasta arithmetic is dear. In Ragu a Poseidon permutation over Pallas is about 192 gates and a Pasta multiplication one gate, while a bit-oriented hash would cost a gate per bit operation. In Kishu a BLAKE3 compression is 11,000 digits, one per bit, and a Pasta multiplication 170 or 374 digits by relation, since the field is not Pasta’s. That is why the recovery circuit is 3.2 million digits against 570,000 Pasta gates, and why Zoodles, with no Pasta arithmetic, suits it. Kishu is not specialized to Pasta at all. Given that, it does well on Pasta in prover time, as the frontier page’s transaction measure shows, and it would do as well on any large-field arithmetic.
  • The claim field is small. Ragu’s claims are Pallas elements; Kishu’s are elements of the 64-bit field’s quadratic extension, 16 bytes, so a Pasta value is proved through limbs or a fingerprint.
  • The step is larger and its size is a knob. Ragu’s step is fixed at 213 coefficients; Kishu’s is 2rank digits over a range of ranks, and one Kishu step holds several of Tachyon’s circuits, as the Zoodles page’s packing shows.
  • The merge verifies a lattice fold. Ragu’s merge circuits verify Pedersen-IPA accumulation with Poseidon transcripts over Pallas (the frontier page’s circuit budget); Kishu’s verify Akita’s fold, its sum-checks and images, with a BLAKE3 or Poseidon transcript in digits, as above.
  • Zero knowledge by masking. Ragu rerandomizes its proofs in two steps of their own; Kishu’s accumulation is made zero-knowledge by a masking fold with rejection sampling, paid once per transaction, as the zero-knowledge note describes.
