Spend authorization

A Zoodles spend is authorized in one of two ways, chosen per input and usually the same for all of a transaction’s inputs. The first is a hash preimage: knowledge of the secret behind the note’s payment key, proved inside the spend’s own step. The second is a hash-based signature, leanSPHINCS, made outside the proof and verified inside the host’s transaction. Neither uses a curve. Both serve a native Zoodles spend and a recovery spend of an Ironwood or a Tachyon note, whether or not the spend is made from a hardware wallet. The frontier page prices both as applications of its transaction prover: the preimage statement as the device statement, one BLAKE3 compression, and the leanSPHINCS verifier with BLAKE3, BLAKE2s, or Keccak.

Two methods are needed because signers differ. The hash preimage is what ZIP 2005 already specifies. It is much the more efficient for a signer that creates the transaction itself, with no separation between the device that holds the spending key and the one that builds the proof. The same holds for a signer that is not constrained in outgoing bandwidth or memory. The check is a hash inside a step it proves anyway. The leanSPHINCS signature is feasible on a wider range of devices, since signing is hashing alone and the signature is a few kilobytes. So it reaches an airgapped wallet on a QR channel or a secure element. It may also be compatible with Ethereum’s post-quantum signature, depending on the details of what Ethereum chooses. A third method, a signature whose verification is built for the circuit, is analysed on the CAPSS page.

The pages of this section:

  • Hash preimage: the statement, and why it has to be a signature of knowledge when it is made outside the transaction’s own proof.
  • leanSPHINCS: the signature, its pruned key, and its verifier’s cost in the circuit.
  • CAPSS: a SNARK-friendly signature as a third method, analysed and not adopted: the method for a prime-field proof system, and for Kishu a second signature route with another assumption and no clear gain.
  • Recovery from Ironwood: ZIP 2005’s Recovery Statement, and how the two methods fit it.
  • Recovery from Tachyon: Tachyon’s key structure, what it lacks for recovery, and the migration transaction.
  • Hardware wallets: what a wallet proves on its own under either method, and at what cost.

Quantum recovery

The two recovery pages share one definition. A note is quantum-recoverable when its owner can spend it, or move it to a post-quantum pool, after discrete logarithms fall, by a statement whose soundness rests on hash and lattice assumptions alone. That asks four things of the note and of the chain:

  • the note commits to an owner key qk=H(qsk) whose secret qsk is in no key used to view or to scan, so that such a key does not become a spending key when the curve’s keys do;
  • the commitment’s opening and the derivation of the note’s nullifier can be proved without discrete log, which means hash commitments, or commitments whose derivation is constrained so that a hash binds them;
  • the note’s membership in the chain’s history and its nullifier’s absence from it can be proved from a hash-based structure over the published commitments and nullifiers, built from public data where the chain’s own structure is discrete-log-based;
  • and the spend is authorized by one of the two methods above, with the message bound into the proof.

ZIP 2005 gives Ironwood-pool notes all four, with the quantum spending key and the Recovery Statement. Tachyon’s notes have the hash commitments and the hash-based nullifier by design and lack the owner key, which the Tachyon page takes up.

Hash preimage

The simplest authorization method is Sprout’s: the note’s payment key is a hash of the authorizing key, and the spender proves knowledge of the preimage. The preimage and its image are a quantum spending key and a quantum key as ZIP 2005 defines them [ZIP-2005], qk=Hqk(qsk) by the ZIP’s BLAKE3 derivation.1 Each protocol has keys of its own; what they share is the derivation, so the same check serves:

  • a native Zoodles spend, where qk is the owner component of the note’s payment key;
  • the recovery of an Ironwood note on the use_qsk=true path, where it is the arm SoKqsk of the Recovery Statement; and
  • the recovery of a Tachyon note, once its proof-authorizing key carries qk.

In Zoodles the spend step opens the payment key to (nk,qk) and derives qk from qsk, two BLAKE3 compressions, the second being the check. On its own the statement is one BLAKE3 compression, 11,200 committed digits in Kishu, which the frontier page prices as the device statement qk, with the linking commitment of ZIP 2005’s hardware-wallet section left out for now. Hardware wallets gives what it costs a wallet to prove by itself.

Inside a transaction’s own proof the check needs nothing more: the spend step that proves it is bound to the rest of the transaction by the proof tree, directly and through the PCD headers, so no digest of the transaction is involved. Made outside that proof, as a wallet’s leaf handed to the host or as ZIP 2005’s SoKqsk on the transaction’s SigHash, the proof is a signature, and the rest of this page is about what that requires.

The signature of knowledge

A proof of knowledge of a preimage of qk is not enough. It would verify under any transaction, so it could be replayed; the statement has to be signed. The reason goes deeper than replay. The reduction that proves SoKqsk unforgeable, as a signature scheme with key qk, has to answer signing queries without qsk. So it simulates them, and it must then extract a preimage from a forger who has seen simulated proofs. That is simulation extractability, which plain knowledge soundness does not give. A signature of knowledge is by definition a simulation-extractable proof with the message as its label [CL06].

The folklore technique, and where it is proved

The technique is to bind the message into the Fiat–Shamir transcript from the start. The instance and the message go into the hash before the first challenge, and the chain of challenges binds everything after. Classically this is proved. For sigma protocols it is [FKMV12]. For multi-round sum-check protocols it is recent. [DG23] shows Spartan and Bulletproofs simulation-extractable with no change. [FFKRZ23] and [KPT23] prove it for Fiat–Shamir of a polynomial IOP with a binding commitment in general, under the conditions one expects: the instance hashed first, and a unique-response or state-restoration property of the protocol. The Frozen Heart vulnerabilities of 2022 [TOB22], forgeries against implementations that left the instance out of the hash, are what omitting it costs. The technique is free.

What is missing is the quantum random-oracle model, which Zoodles and the Recovery Protocol need. Fiat–Shamir of sigma protocols is settled there, by [DFMS19] and [LZ19]. Knowledge soundness of Fiat–Shamir on an IOP is settled with polynomial loss, by [CMS19]. But the multi-round measure-and-reprogram bound [DFM20] loses a factor exponential in the number of rounds, which for thirty sum-check rounds says nothing. And the simulation-extractability proofs above rewind, which the quantum setting does not allow. We know of no simulation-extractability result for a sum-check-based succinct argument in the quantum random-oracle model with usable bounds. In the trust-boundary style of the Ironwood formalization, the signature-of-knowledge property would have to be a named hypothesis.

A route that is available: the non-injectivity of the hash

A classical argument avoids simulation extractability altogether, and it fits this statement unusually well. Hqk maps 256 bits to 256 bits, so a uniformly random qsk has a second preimage with probability about 1−1/e, 63 percent. The reduction to the collision resistance of Hqk picks qsk itself, answers every signing query with the real prover, and extracts a preimage from the forgery. A zero-knowledge proof is witness indistinguishable [FS90]. So when a second preimage exists, the forger’s view is the same whichever preimage the reduction holds, and the extracted one differs from the reduction’s with probability about a half. Then the reduction holds a collision. The loss is a factor of about 3.2. This is the two-witness form that [KW03] used for tight signature reductions, with the hash’s own non-injectivity standing in for the second key, so the circuit does not change. It needs zero knowledge and knowledge soundness with auxiliary input, the honest signatures on other messages being that input. Both are available in the quantum random-oracle model for the proof systems in play, and the message is still bound into the instance before the first challenge. Nothing in the protocol changes; only the proof does. This is the proof to write for the Kishu route. The hash-based signature route does not raise the question. leanSPHINCS is a signature scheme with its own strong unforgeability proof, 127 classical bits in the random-oracle model [Wam26], and the message enters its digest with the randomizer.

leanSPHINCS

The second authorization method is a stateless hash-based signature on a digest of the transaction, made outside the proof and verified inside the host’s transaction. The signature and the public key are witnesses, which the zero-knowledge fold hides, so spends stay unlinkable and no re-randomized signature is needed. The scheme is leanSPHINCS, the signature of post-quantum Ethereum [EIP-8288] [Lit26]. A signature is 4,276 bytes with [Wam26]’s pruned key of lifetime 230, the configuration priced here, 6,332 with its layered forest key, and 7,740 with Ethereum’s provisional set. Signing is hashing alone. The pruned key adds 16,384 grinding digests per signature, and its proved lifetime is 126,900 signatures, one per transaction. The grind is the signer’s, since it is keyed and the key cannot leave the signer without revealing which leaves it kept; a full tree with a helper building and storing it has no grind, which Hardware wallets takes up.

The message

Since the signature is made outside the proof, its message has to bind the transaction’s effecting data. In Zoodles it is a BLAKE3 digest of them: each spend’s two nullifiers, each output’s commitment, the change commitment, the fee, and the epoch, 235 bytes or 4 compressions. The digest is a PCD header value: each spend verifies its signature over it, and the fee step recomputes it from the nullifiers and commitments that its children’s headers carry. The verification, not the digest, is the expensive part of the method. In ZIP 2005’s Recovery Statement [ZIP-2005] the message is the SigHash.

The verifier in the circuit

The host proves the verifier inside its transaction: 298 BLAKE3 or BLAKE2s compressions, or 262 Keccak-f permutations, for the pruned key, against 462 compressions or 408 permutations for the layered one and 515 permutations for Ethereum’s. XOR is not free in a digit arithmetization, so in Kishu a BLAKE3 compression is 11,000 committed bits, a BLAKE2s compression 15,800, and a Keccak-f permutation 92,200. The verifier is therefore 3.38 million digits with BLAKE3 and 4.74 million with BLAKE2s, so BLAKE3’s is 71 percent of BLAKE2s’s, since its compression has seven rounds to BLAKE2s’s ten. With Keccak it is 24.2 million, 5.1 times BLAKE2s’s, which is Ethereum’s open hash question seen from the circuit. In a Boolean circuit with XOR free the Keccak-to-BLAKE2s ratio is 3.3. With zero knowledge Kishu proves the BLAKE3 verifier in 0.173 s on one M4 core at rank 20, the BLAKE2s one in 0.222 s at rank 21, and the Keccak one in 0.917 s at rank 22, beside 0.220 s for the recovery circuit itself. Ethereum’s draft fixes Keccak-256 as the scheme’s only primitive, and the circuit and the device both argue against it. If Ethereum keeps Keccak, there is no compatibility to gain from BLAKE2s either, and the choice is between Keccak and BLAKE3, Zoodles’ own hash and the cheapest of the three in the circuit. On the device BLAKE3’s compression has fewer rounds than BLAKE2s’s, though [Wam26]’s benchmark did not measure it.

CAPSS

A third authorization method, which Zoodles does not adopt, is a SNARK-friendly post-quantum signature: one whose verification is cheap inside a proof because its hashing is a permutation that is cheap in the proof system at hand, rather than a bit-oriented hash. CAPSS [FR25] is a framework for such signatures, and the one suggested by Tachyon’s book. The signature is a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of a preimage under a one-way function built by truncating the permutation, made with SmallWood [FR25a], a hash-based argument whose Merkle trees and transcript hashing use the same permutation. Its security rests on that permutation alone, modelled as ideal, plus the random-oracle heuristic for the sponge. The paper instantiates it with Anemoi, Griffin, Poseidon, and Rescue-Prime, but the framework takes any permutation; which one is a question for the proof system that verifies the signature.

The paper’s figures

Over a 256-bit field at 128 bits, the paper’s instances are between 9,504 and 25,824 bytes, with verification between 20,717 and 71,145 rank-1 constraints. Its headline instances are Anemoi’s, 12,640 bytes and 23,484 constraints at the default trade-off, with verification calling the permutation about 173 times and signing about 13,900. Over the 64-bit Goldilocks field, which is Kishu’s size, the implemented Anemoi instance signs in 101 ms and verifies in 1.4 ms on a desktop core at 9,715 bytes, against 2,460 ms of signing over a 254-bit field. The paper estimates the 64-bit verifier at 80,000 to 100,000 constraints, about 4 times the 256-bit field’s, since the smaller field needs more repetitions for the same soundness.

Anemoi is not the permutation to use. The algebraic FreeLunch attacks [BBL+24] and the Gröbner-basis cryptanalysis of Anemoi that followed [CR25] have cut its margin, and Griffin’s and Rescue-Prime’s with it, below the 128 bits the paper’s parameters claim. The paper says so and keeps its parameters for comparability. Its Poseidon instances, which the attacks do not reach, are the conservative ones: 19,616 bytes and 46,567 constraints at the default trade-off, with verification calling the permutation about 143 times at three widths and signing about 10,000.

An instance for Kishu

A SNARK-friendly signature’s advantage is in a prime-field arithmetization: there a CAPSS verifier is tens of thousands of multiplication gates, where a leanSPHINCS verifier’s 298 BLAKE3 or BLAKE2s compressions are millions. Kishu commits bits, which is what suits BLAKE2s to it, and a field wire costs it 22 digits, so the comparison has to be made in Kishu’s own units. The permutation that is cheap in Kishu is Poseidon over its 64-bit field, which the model already prices at 276 multiplications a permutation, each a committed wire. Taking the paper’s Poseidon call counts and its factor of 4 for the 64-bit field, a verifier is about 3.47 million digits, against 3.38 million for leanSPHINCS with BLAKE3 and 4.74 million with BLAKE2s. The paper’s own constraint estimate for the 64-bit field, at one wire a constraint, gives 2.2 million. So in Kishu the two are within a factor of two or so of each other, and nothing like the order of magnitude a prime-field circuit sees. These are estimates from the paper’s counts at the model’s per-permutation cost, not a row of the frontier page. A row would count the verifier’s calls at each width and add the field arithmetic of the PACS checks.

Signing is a SmallWood proof, about 40,000 permutations over the 64-bit field with Merkle trees of 2^10 to 2^14 leaves. At the page’s assumed rate for an MCU-class device that is about 1.1 s, and a few times that on a secure element. So a device can sign with it, where it could not make a Kishu leaf. The trees’ memory, 2^12 leaves of 32 bytes, is a secure element’s whole budget. The signature, about 20 kbytes, fits a QR channel at four or five times leanSPHINCS’s scanning time.

Against the other two methods

  • In the circuit. Parity with leanSPHINCS within a factor of two or so, on the estimates above, rather than a gain.
  • On the device. Seconds of signing at the MCU rate and tens of kilobytes of memory, against hashing alone and under a second of grinding for leanSPHINCS; still feasible, which a Kishu leaf is not.
  • The assumption. The hash preimage and leanSPHINCS rest on a bit-oriented hash. CAPSS rests on an arithmetization-oriented permutation, the class whose margins the algebraic attacks have cut and which the frontier page excludes from its default hash policy for future-proofing. Poseidon is the member with the most scrutiny, and a signature key can be rotated where a long-lived commitment cannot, which makes the policy’s case weaker here than for storage.
  • Ethereum. Ethereum’s post-quantum signature is leanSPHINCS, so the compatibility the second method may offer is not on this route.

So CAPSS is the method for a prime-field proof system, and for Kishu it is a second signature route with a different assumption and no clear gain over leanSPHINCS. It is not priced as a row; a row would be a day’s work if the comparison needed settling.

  • [FR25a] Thibauld Feneuil, Matthieu Rivain. SmallWood: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments and Zero-Knowledge Arguments for Relatively Small Instances. 2025. https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1085

Recovery from Ironwood

ZIP 2005 makes Ironwood-pool notes quantum-recoverable in the sense of this section’s definition [ZIP-2005]. Each note’s keys commit to a quantum key qk=Hqk(qsk), the quantum spending key qsk derived from the spending key and in no viewing key. A Recovery Statement, to be introduced in a later upgrade, spends such a note without discrete logarithms. The statement needs two authorizations of a recovery spend. One is a RedDSA signature under the randomized key, which FROST makes t-of-n. The other is SoKqsk: a signature of knowledge of qsk on the transaction’s SigHash, with Hqk(qsk)=qk, which is the hash preimage method made as a signature. With use_qsk=true the rest of the statement is proved from viewing-key material, the path a hardware wallet is meant to optimize. The other path, use_qsk=false, has the statement prove the key derivations from the spending key itself. The recovery circuit the frontier page prices takes either value, as ZIP 2005’s statement does, the two paths’ derivations multiplexed over the same three BLAKE2b compressions; this section’s hardware-wallet analysis follows the use_qsk=true path. In a Zoodles transaction the recovery spends also reveal their total, for the pool accounting that the Zoodles page sets out.

With FROST, ZIP 2005 has the participants agree privately on the value sk from which nk, qsk, and qk are derived, while ak is the output of the distributed key generation. Every wallet then holds the same qsk. So against an adversary who breaks discrete logarithms the recovery spend’s unforgeability is that of SoKqsk as a signature scheme with key qk, 1-of-n, while a pre-quantum adversary corrupting up to t−1 wallets is bounded by re-randomized FROST; Hardware wallets sets out that model. The frontier page prices the recovery circuit as an application: in Kishu with zero knowledge it takes 0.220 s on one core at rank 21.

The signature method as an arm of the Recovery Statement

What a leanSPHINCS route asks of ZIP 2005 is less than it first seems. Its qk=Hqk(qsk) hashes the secret, and a hash-based signature needs qk to commit to the signature’s public key instead. Deriving that key from the seed inside the Recovery Statement would cost the top layer’s key generation, out of the question. But the derivation is domain-separated. A signature route would define its own derivation of qk from the public key under another context, and the Recovery Statement, which is not yet specified, would accept it as one more arm of its tagged union beside the preimage proof and SoKsk. The arms cannot satisfy each other’s rule, since that would be a collision across two domain-separated hashes. So nothing has to be decided before the scheme is known. The one consequence is that a key derived before the signature route exists is a preimage-route key. A wallet that wants the signature route later needs a new key, which means new addresses and moved funds.

References

  • [ZIP-2005] Daira-Emma Hopwood, Jack Grigg. ZIP 2005: Ironwood Quantum Recoverability. https://zips.z.cash/zip-2005

Recovery from Tachyon

Tachyon is designed to be quantum-private today and quantum-sound after an upgrade [Tac26]. Zoodles is that upgrade, defined here.

Tachyon’s owner field is a Poseidon commitment over Pallas, pk=Com(ak,nk), to the spend validating key and the nullifier deriving key. Its note commitment cm=Com(pk,v,ψ;rcm) is a Poseidon commitment, with no constraint needed on how rcm is derived, and its nullifiers are hash outputs. So a quantum computer learns nothing from the chain, and the commitment and nullifier parts of this section’s definition hold by design. The only curve points on chain are the value commitments and the randomized keys, and re-randomization keeps those private too. What a quantum computer can do is forge: take the discrete log of a randomized key and authorize a spend, or break the discrete-log polynomial commitments of the proof system. Tachyon’s book sketches a full upgrade, a post-quantum signature proved in zero knowledge in place of re-randomization and a lattice folding scheme in place of Pedersen, and leaves it there.

What the key structure lacks

Recovery before or across that upgrade is the question for Zoodles, and there Tachyon’s key structure has a gap that Ironwood’s does not. The witness for Tachyon’s quantum recoverability is the opening of pk, the pair (ak,nk). Tachyon has no viewing keys as such, but nk plays the part of one: a host that scans for a hardware wallet holds it to derive the nullifiers, and holding it must not authorize a spend. And ak is the public output of a FROST group’s key generation. So once discrete logarithms fall, the recovery witness is in the wrong hands in both settings: a single-signer hardware wallet’s host holds nk and ak, so it could spend; and a FROST group has no secret that only its members hold, since ask is shared and never reconstructed and ak is known to every participant. ZIP 2005 avoids both by committing to a separate qk=Hqk(qsk) whose secret is in no viewing key, and by having a FROST group derive qsk from a privately agreed value [ZIP-2005]. Tachyon has no counterpart, a regression from Ironwood for single-signer hardware wallets and FROST groups alike.

The suggested change

The fix is small. The proof-authorizing key becomes (ak,nk,qk) with qk=Hqk(qsk), ZIP 2005’s BLAKE3 derivation, and the owner field pk=Com(ak,nk,qk) stays one hash commitment: Tachyon’s sponge absorbs four field elements a permutation and pk takes three, so qk fits as the fourth, entered as one Pallas element by reduction modulo p, since a 256-bit hash output is not one. The ordinary spend circuit is unchanged, since it opens pk as before with qk as one more field. The recovery statement proves knowledge of qsk and nk rather than of ak and nk, and a FROST group derives qsk from its privately agreed value as ZIP 2005 prescribes, with ak still the distributed key generation’s output. The cost is one more field in the commitment and, in the recovery proof, one BLAKE3 compression, 11,200 Kishu digits, which the recovery circuit application already charges for Hqk, and the reduction’s range check of 256 bits.

The migration transaction

A Tachyon note moves to Zoodles by a recovery spend and a Zoodles output. The transaction reveals the total it spends from the Tachyon pool, for the pool accounting that the Zoodles page sets out. The spend proves knowledge of qsk against qk in pk, the Poseidon openings of pk and cm over Pallas, the membership of cm in a hash-based tree over Tachyon’s published commitments, and the nullifier’s derivation and its absence from Tachyon’s published nullifiers. It cannot rely on Tachyon’s set polynomials, which are Pedersen commitments, once discrete log is gone, so the tree is the structure for Tachyon’s notes as it is for Zoodles’ own epochs. The shape is ZIP 2005’s Recovery Statement over Tachyon’s note format, with Poseidon where Orchard has Sinsemilla. Pricing it as an application of the frontier page is pending; it is also why Tachyon’s circuits are priced in each post-quantum proof system there.

  • [ZIP-2005] Daira-Emma Hopwood, Jack Grigg. ZIP 2005: Ironwood Quantum Recoverability. https://zips.z.cash/zip-2005

Hardware wallets

A hardware wallet can use either authorization method of this section on its own: the hash preimage as a Kishu leaf of the transaction’s proof, or a leanSPHINCS signature that the host verifies in its transaction. This page asks what the wallet has to compute and transfer for each, and what a channel allows. It was written for ZIP 2005’s Recovery Statement [ZIP-2005], whose Option A keeps qsk on a hardware wallet and has the networked host prove the rest (Recovery from Ironwood). It takes the device split from an analysis of FROST members recovering from a seed phrase. The costs are the same for a native Zoodles spend. The figures come from the PCS frontier page, which prices the wallet’s part as applications of its transaction measure.

The device split

The model to reason in makes the hardware wallets the only honest parties and treats every networked device as the adversary. A wallet holds the spending key sk, or with FROST its signing share and the common sk, and so qsk. It exports nk and qk and nothing else that is derived from the secret. ak is derived from sk and exported by a single-signer wallet; with FROST it is the output of the distributed key generation. rivk_ext and the incoming and outgoing viewing keys follow from those, so the host can scan, build transactions and produce the main Recovery proof, whose witness is viewing-key material plus the note and its path. ZIP 2005’s other path, use_qsk=false, has the Recovery Statement prove the key derivations from sk itself. The priced circuit takes either value; this page follows the use_qsk=true path, the one whose costs a hardware wallet is meant to optimize.

The wallet signs FROST shares and makes SoKqsk, each after verifying the transaction and asking the user, and the user’s confirmation is the adversary’s choice of message. Two adversary classes share one win condition: a consensus-valid recovery spend on an unapproved SigHash.

  • A pre-quantum adversary corrupts up to t−1 wallets. It is bounded by the unforgeability of re-randomized FROST.
  • A discrete-log-breaking adversary is given every host’s state and every network message, but no wallet. It is bounded by the unforgeability of SoKqsk as a signature scheme with key qk. That bound is 1-of-n, since every wallet holds the same qsk.

Option A is the statement that the second class learns nothing from a wallet but its interface’s outputs.

What the wallet can prove

Two shapes are priced. The wallet can prove the preimage statement as a leaf of the transaction’s own proof system, Kishu on the frontier page: one BLAKE3 compression, 11,200 committed digits, with the linking commitment of ZIP 2005’s hardware-wallet section left out for now. Or the wallet can sign with leanSPHINCS and leave the verification to the host, which proves the verifier inside its own transaction with the signature and the public key as witnesses, so the spends stay unlinkable.

A Kishu leaf

The handoff is the whole question. The host folds the wallet’s leaf into the transaction’s accumulator, and split accumulation needs the witness of whatever it folds. So the wallet hands over a masked witness: the response z=y+cs of the zero-knowledge note (the zk note), a Gaussian mask y added to the leaf’s digits s under a challenge c. Rejection sampling makes the accepted z independent of the secret. The mask covers the leaf’s 2rank digits alone, since the wallet hands over no accumulator of its own. The transaction measure charges the user’s handoff the host’s merge that folds the leaf, and a small merge of the handoff’s own: the challenge derivation, the commitment identity, and the claim fold. The decomposition and the range and norm proofs are deferred to the host (the zk note’s §5.8). For a one-compression leaf the host’s merge is most of the cost. The measure’s 0.0266 s at rank 16 is 88 percent merge and 12 percent fold, and the circuit itself is a few percent.

The wallet need not prove that fold. The zk note’s §4.2 lists the handoff merge’s witness as simulatable: the hiding commitment, the mask’s commitment, the challenge, the claims and the obligation transcripts. So the host can derive the challenge, prove the fold’s merge and the obligations (the zk note’s §5.8 deferral), and verify the leaf’s sum-checks in its own merge. The wallet keeps what touches the secret. It commits the leaf with a hiding padding at the masked rank. It proves its constraint and Booleanity sum-checks under Libra-style masking polynomials, since the host sees their transcripts: 112 committed elements of Fq​. Each is committed in the widest digits that keep the vector’s matrix at the padding sweep’s rows, judged by the vector’s exact ℓ2​ norm: 33 balanced dibits at the 147-bit floor, and 22 tribits at 128. It samples and commits the mask in idle time, and computes the response with the rejection test.

The padding is computational rather than the zk note’s leftover-hash one. Aρ for ρ of 4,800 uniform bits at the 147-bit floor, the page’s default, or 4,400 at 128, is pseudorandom if knapsack-LWE is hard at the commitment’s rows. By the Micciancio–Mol duality that is LWE of the padding’s bits less the rows, with the rows as samples and binary secret and error at the 64-bit modulus (the zk note’s §5.10 gives the argument). The lattice estimator puts the cheapest attack on the padding at the matrix’s 1,024 rows at 149 and 128 quantum bits at the two floors’ paddings, under the page’s cost model, a dual hybrid attack on the binary secret. The primal attacks are a hundred bits dearer, so a primal estimate alone would overstate the margin. The padding is the least on the sweep’s grid, 50 bits where the floors are crossed, that reaches the floor, so the hedge of the 147-bit floor applies to it too. At the zk note’s 1,385 rows 5,000 bits give 140 bits, and at 2,048 rows they would fall short of the 128-bit floor. The statistical padding would be 66 thousand bits, 5.9 times the statement.

So the wallet commits 19,700 digits. That is 0.223 ms of online work on one M4 core, under a tenth of the handoff fold that the measure charges the user, with 0.278 ms in idle time, and a response of 54 kbytes at 22 bits a coordinate. The device rates are assumptions, scaled from the hash rates that [Wam26]’s hardware-wallet benchmark measured on a Ledger Nano S+: 10 million word multiplications a second for an MCU-class device and 3 million for a secure element. At those rates the computation takes 0.067 and 0.22 s. The transfer of z at that device’s measured 21 kbytes a second over USB takes 2.6 s, or 0.93 s with a pipelined transport. No merge circuit and no accumulator sit on the device, and the witness is 2.9 kbytes packed at its digits’ widths. So a Kishu signature of knowledge is within reach of a high-end hardware wallet on a USB link, and the transfer is the larger part of it.

Over an animated QR code

An airgapped wallet of the Keystone kind exchanges data by animated QR codes, fountain-coded fragments read by a phone camera from the wallet’s screen. Keystone’s firmware sends fragments of 200 bytes at 5 frames a second, 1 kbyte a second. So the response takes 54 s with no frame missed, and the fountain code’s redundancy after missed frames can double or treble that. Denser codes would cut it: a fragment of 800 bytes at the same rate gives 14 s, and the format’s ceiling, a version-40 symbol holding about 2,100 bytes of fragment, 5.2 s. Whether a camera reads the denser codes reliably depends on the screen, the light, and the camera, and gets worse toward the ceiling. So the transfer is slow at today’s settings and within reach with denser codes on some devices. The device’s memory is the other constraint: it holds the mask, about 54 kbytes, over which the response is written in place, beside the witness. The response cannot be made much smaller, and the reason is not an encoding choice. The accepted z is a Gaussian of width σ on every coordinate of the leaf, about log2​(σ2πe​) bits of information each. It is secret-dependent, so it cannot be regenerated from a seed as the mask can. With no padding and no masking elements the leaf’s own 11,200 coordinates still make 29 kbytes. A succinct Kishu proof of the leaf in place of the response would be about 72 kbytes, whatever the rank from 14 up, since nearly all of it is the opening’s fixed parts, the compression levels and the terminal. A narrower mask saves two or three bits a coordinate at the price of idle-time attempts, and a lighter challenge set a fraction of a bit. The transfer cannot be avoided by moving the fold elsewhere: split accumulation needs the host to hold a witness of the wallet’s accumulator, and that witness is z. A wallet on today’s QR settings is better served by the signature of the next section.

A hash-based signature

leanSPHINCS fits the QR channel: a signature of 4,276 bytes with the pruned key, 6,332 with the layered forest key, or 7,740 with Ethereum’s provisional set [EIP-8288] [Lit26] is a few seconds of scanning. Its signing is hashing alone, measured on a Nano S+ by [Wam26]’s benchmark. The pruned key’s 16,384 grinding digests per signature take 2.8 s with Keccak on that device and 0.50 s with BLAKE2s; BLAKE3, with seven rounds to BLAKE2s’s ten, was not in the benchmark and should be no slower. The grind is the wallet’s: it is keyed, and the key cannot leave the wallet without revealing which leaves it kept. A full tree can take the host’s help instead. The wallet produces the leaf hashes at key generation, the host builds and stores the tree and supplies the authentication paths, and signing then has no grind.

leanSPHINCS is stateless and deterministic, which matters when every member’s wallet holds the same seed: a stateful scheme’s index would be reused across wallets, and the deterministic randomizer makes the members’ signatures identical. The verifier’s cost in the host’s transaction is on the leanSPHINCS page.
